notes: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth: This statement summarizes the entire creation account (Genesis 1:3-2). Already a key question—Who created the world?—is answered (see also Proverbs 8:22-31; John 1:1-3). Although the modern naturalistic mindset rejects this question and that of creation’s purpose, Genesis affirms God’s role and purpose in creation. • The common name for God (Hebrew ’elohim) emphasizes his grand supremacy. The word ’elohim is plural, but the verbs used with it are usually singular, reflecting the consistent scriptural proclamation of a single, all-powerful God. • created (Hebrew bara’): In the Old Testament, God is always the agent of creation expressed by this verb. It describes the making of something fresh and new—notably the cosmos (Genesis 1:1, Genesis 1:21; Genesis 2:3), humankind (Genesis 1:27), the Israelite nation (Isaiah 43:1), and the future new creation (Isaiah 65:17). • The heavens and the earth are the entire ordered cosmos.

These verses introduce the Pentateuch (Genesis—Deuteronomy) and teach Israel that the world was created, ordered, and populated by the one true God and not by the gods of surrounding nations. • God blessed three specific things: animal life (Genesis 1:22-25), human life (Genesis 1:27), and the Sabbath day (Genesis 2:3). This trilogy of blessings highlights the Creator’s plan: Humankind was made in God’s image to enjoy sovereign dominion over the creatures of the earth and to participate in God’s Sabbath rest.

This verse gives the background for the summary in Genesis 1:1 and the detailed description in Genesis 1:3-2. God’s creative utterances bring order to the chaotic state of the universe. • formless . . . empty (Hebrew tohu . . . bohu): This terse idiom means something like “wild and waste.” It sets a stark contrast to the final ordered state of the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1). • deep waters (Hebrew tehom): Some scholars say this alludes to the Mesopotamian goddess Tiamat (representing chaos), but Genesis views tehom as inhospitable chaos, not as a deity or goddess that God engaged in cosmic battle. • the Spirit of God: God directly superintended the creation process.

Then God said: Nothing in ch Genesis 1:1-31 is created apart from God’s powerful word (cp. Psalm 33:6, Psalm 33:9). • “Let there be . . .” and there was: God’s command enacted his will to create the world. God is not a part of creation or limited by it; he is the supreme ruler over everything (cp. Nehemiah 9:6).
In the first three days, God formed the chaos into a habitable world.

Light is antithetical to chaotic darkness (Genesis 1:2); the light is declared good but the darkness is not (cp. John 1:5). God is the source of this light (cp. Genesis 1:14-19). God separated the light, as he did water (cp. Genesis 1:6-8), by his creative word. Light is associated with life and blessing (Job 38:19-20; Psalm 19:1-6; Psalm 97:11; Psalm 104:19-20; Isaiah 60:19-20) and sets a boundary on the darkness that would destroy cosmic order. Darkness often typifies terror, death, and evil (see Genesis 15:12; Job 18:6, Job 18:18; Psalm 88:12; Ephesians 5:11-12; 1 Jn 1:5).

God called (or named): To name something is to exercise authority over it (see also Genesis 2:19-20). • day: The Hebrew yom can refer to daylight (Genesis 1:5), to a 24-hour period (Genesis 1:5), or to an unspecified time period (Genesis 2:4, “When,” literally in the day; cp. Exodus 20:8-11). • evening . . . morning: The Hebrew day began at sundown, just as the first day began with darkness and brought the first morning light.

The creation account describes the appearance of things from a human perspective. The sky is viewed as a shiny dome that is a buffer between two collections of water (cp. Job 37:18; Ezekiel 1:22). In the ancient Near East, the cosmos was understood as a three-tier system, with rain originating from the outermost tier (see Genesis 7:11-12 and study note).

Let the waters . . . flow together: Other ancient cultures viewed the sea as a hostile force. Genesis shows God as further restraining chaos (see study note on 1:2) by prescribing specific boundaries for the sea. The flood—an act of God’s judgment (Genesis 6:7)—undid these boundaries and returned the earth to chaos (Genesis 7:1-24).

Let them . . . mark the seasons, days, and years: The movement of the heavenly bodies defined Israel’s liturgical calendar, whose roots in creation gave a sacred timing to Israel’s festivals and celebrations (see Exodus 23:15; Leviticus 23:4).
On days 4–6, God filled the domains that had been formed during days 1–3 (Genesis 1:3-13).

In the surrounding pagan cultures, the two great lights were worshiped as deities, but in Genesis they serve God and humanity (see Psalm 136:7-9; Jeremiah 31:35). The sun and moon are not named; they are simply called the larger one and the smaller one. Not including their names may have reminded Israel that they were not gods. • govern: Cp. Genesis 1:26, Genesis 1:28; Psalm 136:9. • the stars: The starry heavens testify to God’s creative power as they proclaim his glory (Psalm 19:1; Psalm 148:3). They do not predict the future, as Israel’s neighbors believed (see Jeremiah 10:2).

Contrary to the pagan idea that the great sea creatures were co-eternal with God, Genesis states that God created them and is sovereign over them. The Hebrew word tanninim (“creatures”) elsewhere refers to crocodiles (Ezekiel 29:3), powerful monsters (Jeremiah 51:34), or the sea creature Leviathan (Isaiah 27:1; cp. Job 41:1-34).

God blessed them: God’s blessing commissions and enables the fulfillment of what God has spoken (see “Blessing” Theme Note). • Let the fish . . . let the birds: These directives define the blessing. The fish and birds are fertile by God’s command, not by pagan ritual, as some of Israel’s neighbors thought.

Let us make is more personal than the remote “Let there be” (e.g., Genesis 1:3, Genesis 1:6). • The plural us has inspired several explanations: (1) the Trinity; (2) the plural to denote majesty; (3) a plural to show deliberation with the self; and (4) God speaking with his heavenly court of angels. The concept of the Trinity—one true God who exists eternally in three distinct persons—was revealed at a later stage in redemptive history, making it unlikely that the human author intended that here. Hebrew scholars generally dismiss the plural of majesty view because the grammar does not clearly support it (the plural of majesty has not been demonstrated to be communicated purely through a plural verb). The plural of self-deliberation also lacks evidence; the only clear examples refer to Israel as a corporate unity (e.g., 2 Sam 24:14). God’s speaking to the heavenly court, however, is well-attested in the Old Testament (see Genesis 3:22; Genesis 11:7; 1 Kgs 22:19-22; Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-6; Job 38:7; Psalm 89:5-6; Isaiah 6:1-8; Daniel 10:12-13). • The descriptors in our image and like us are virtually synonymous in Hebrew. Humans enjoy a unique relationship with God. • They will reign: Humans represent the Creator as his ambassadors, vice-regents, and administrators on earth.

The first poetry of Genesis reflectively celebrates God’s climactic feat in creating humankind. • human beings: This term (Hebrew ha-’adam, “the man”) is often used to denote humanity collectively (see Genesis 6:1, Genesis 6:5-7; Genesis 9:5-6). Though traditionally translated “man,” gender is not at issue here; both male and female are included.

God blessed them: See study note on 1:22; see also Genesis 17:16; Genesis 48:16; Deuteronomy 7:13. • said: God’s message to humankind is direct and intimate; we are stewards of his delegated authority. • govern. . . . Reign: As God’s vice-regents, humans are entrusted with the care and management of the world God created (see also Genesis 9:2; Psalm 8:5-8).
These verses highlight the extent (throughout the earth) and variety (every seed-bearing plant . . . all the fruit trees) of God’s provision for humans, animals, and birds.
The Creator declares his work good seven times in ch Genesis 1:1-31; following the creation of human beings, God declares it all very good.

Humankind is the high point of God’s creative acts (Genesis 1:26-31), while day 7 is the climax of the creation week. When God rested, he endorsed all of creation—there was nothing more to do! This seven-day framework structured Israel’s week, with the seventh day as the precedent for their weekly Sabbath. The Sabbath was intended to celebrate God’s finished work; the seventh day would be set apart as holy and dedicated to the Creator, who also rested (see Exodus 20:8-11; Exodus 31:12-17; cp. Matthew 12:1-8; Romans 14:5-6; Colossians 2:16-17; Hebrews 4:1-11).

The first six days of creation involved separation (light from darkness, day from night, water from dry land). The last act of creation separated what is ordinary from what is holy, thus laying the foundation for Israel’s worship. It also anticipated a coming age of rest (Hebrews 4:1-11; Hebrews 12:2; Hebrews 13:14). • The absence of the usual “morning and evening” reflects the Creator’s willingness to enter into unending fellowship with humankind.

This is the account (literally These are the generations; Hebrew toledoth): This or a similar phrase is repeated throughout Genesis, creating an internal outline for the book. In other occurrences, it introduces the genealogy or story of a key personality (Genesis 5:1; Genesis 6:9; Genesis 10:1; Genesis 11:10, Genesis 11:27; Genesis 25:12, Genesis 25:19; Genesis 36:1; Genesis 37:2). • Some have argued that the first half of Genesis 2:4 belongs with Genesis 1:1–2:3, but it is more likely the introduction to the account that follows. • Lord God (Hebrew Yahweh Elohim) is the second name used for God in the early chapters of Genesis. Elohim (Genesis 1:1–2:3) describes the all-powerful creator God. Yahweh Elohim speaks of the eternal God who formed a lasting covenant with Israel (Exodus 3:6, Exodus 3:13-15). Accordingly, Genesis 2:4-25 focuses on God as provider more than as creator. The three themes of sexuality, dominion, and food in ch Genesis 1:1-31 are now addressed in reverse order (food, Genesis 2:8-17; dominion, Genesis 2:18-20; sexuality, Genesis 2:21-25).

This account (see study note on 2:4) of the heavens and the earth is not a second creation account; rather, it is a theological and historical expansion on Genesis 1:1–2:3. The focus is now on what the cosmos produced rather than on its creation. Special attention is given to the first man and woman. As the story progresses, it is colored by contrasts of good and evil, knowledge and ignorance, life and death, harmony and discord.
cultivate: Work does not result from sin; it was part of the original structure of creation and is directly tied to human identity and purpose (Genesis 1:28; Genesis 2:15).
springs: The word refers to subterranean springs that rose to the surface of the ground.

In Genesis 1:1–2:3, creation happens at a distance, by divine command (“Let there be . . . and that is what happened”). In this account, the creative act is much more intimate (see also Genesis 2:8-9, Genesis 2:21-22). • from the dust of the ground: In Hebrew, ’adamah (“ground”) forms a wordplay with ’adam (“man”). The earth remains the definitive reference point for humans, who in death return to dust (Genesis 3:17-19; Genesis 4:11; Job 4:19; Job 10:8-9; Isaiah 29:16). • breathed . . . into the man’s nostrils: God’s breath is not imparted to other animals; only humans are formed in God’s image (Genesis 1:27) and enjoy dialogue with their Creator (Genesis 2:16-17; Genesis 3:8-13). They alone have spiritual awareness and moral conscience (see Job 32:8).

Eden was the general location in which the garden was placed, not the garden itself. The term could mean “plain,” “delight,” or “fertility.” The description that follows favors the idea of fertility. • in the east: The exact location of Eden is left to speculation, but it was east of Canaan, Israel’s later home. • God placed the man in the garden for divine fellowship and physical blessing (see also Genesis 2:15 and study note there).

Analogous to the sacred time marked out on the seventh day of creation (Genesis 2:2-3), the sacred space of the garden in Eden was separate from the surrounding world. It functioned as a garden-temple or sanctuary because the Lord manifested his presence there in a special way.

Beauty and bounty characterized humanity’s original environment (cp. Genesis 13:10). • The tree of life represented God’s presence and provision. The one who ate of it would have everlasting life (Genesis 3:22), which made it a rich image for later Israelite and Christian reflection (Proverbs 3:18; Proverbs 11:30; Proverbs 13:12; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:2, Revelation 22:14, Revelation 22:19). The candlestick in Israel’s Tabernacle may have been a stylized representation of it (Exodus 25:31-35). • Eating the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil enabled humanity’s capacity for wisdom (Genesis 3:6) and moral discernment (Genesis 3:5, Genesis 3:22; cp. Deuteronomy 1:39, “innocent”). Eating from it represented a human grasp for autonomy and wisdom that were God’s alone (cp. Proverbs 30:1-4). Humans sidestepped God’s revelation as the means of moral discernment, flaunting their independence rather than submitting to God’s will (cp. Proverbs 1:7). Choosing human wisdom over God’s instruction brings death and destruction (see Psalm 19:7-9; Ezekiel 28:6, Ezekiel 28:15-17).

The river that was watering the garden was a material blessing (bringing agricultural fertility) and a symbol of God’s presence (cp. Psalm 46:4; Ezekiel 47:1-12; Zechariah 14:8; Revelation 22:1-2). • dividing into four branches (literally heads): The common understanding is that one river had its source in Eden, flowed down through the garden, and then split into the four rivers named.
This detailed description portrays the eastern region around Eden as a mountain with rivers flowing out to the world. Eden’s beauty and fertility enriched the whole earth.

The Pishon and the Gihon (Genesis 2:13) cannot be identified with certainty. If the land of Havilah was in southeast Arabia or on the African coast, as some biblical data suggest (see Genesis 10:7; Genesis 25:18; 1 Sam 15:7), then the Pishon was possibly the Nile River. Josephus thought that Havilah and the Pishon were in India (Antiquities 1.1.3). Two other proposals suggest: (1) rivers in the mountains of eastern Turkey where the Tigris and Euphrates (Genesis 2:14) also flow, and (2) the marshy delta near the Persian Gulf. Current geographical conditions make any theory impossible to prove conclusively.

The magnificence and fertility of the garden are pictured as spreading to the surrounding regions through the rivers flowing out from it. The four rivers possibly imply that the garden’s bounty flowed out to the four corners of the earth. • Gold and onyx were later used for decorating the Tabernacle, the Temple (Exodus 25:3-9; 1 Chr 29:2), and the priests’ clothing (Exodus 28:9-14, Exodus 28:20). • Resin was used in sacred incense (Exodus 30:34).

Gihon: Though unknown, proposals have included the Nile (as in the Greek version of Jeremiah 2:18; Josephus, Antiquities 1.1.3), the Jordan, or, according to Jewish tradition, a river that formerly ran through the Kidron Valley (1 Kgs 1:33; 2 Chr 33:14). • Although Cush is the name of ancient Ethiopia, Mesopotamian regions associated with Babylon seem to be the immediate setting (see Genesis 10:8); Cush is possibly the land of the Kassites, a dynasty ruling in Babylonia.
Tigris . . . Euphrates: These well-known rivers flow from the mountains of eastern Turkey.

to tend and watch over: The garden required maintenance and oversight. Tending the Garden was humanity’s dignifying work. These roles in God’s garden-sanctuary were later applied to God’s Tabernacle (see Leviticus 8:35; Numbers 3:5-10; Numbers 4:46-49).

except (literally but you must not eat): This prohibition is given in the same legal format as Israel’s Ten Commandments (see Exodus 20:1-17; Deuteronomy 5:6-21). The Lord built law and obedience into the fabric of his covenant relationship with humanity. • the knowledge of good and evil: See study note on 2:9. • you are sure to die: The consequences of disobedience would be immediate spiritual death (loss of relationship with God) and eventual physical death (see Genesis 3:22-23; Ecclesiastes 12:6-7).

It is not good: This is God’s first negative assessment of an otherwise excellent creation (Genesis 1:31). The Lord God is portrayed as a father who obtains a bride for his son (cp. ch Genesis 24:1-67). • The answer to the man’s need is a helper who is just right for him; she is his perfect complement, made in the same image of God (Genesis 1:26-27), given the same commission (Genesis 1:28; Genesis 2:15), and obligated by the same prohibition (Genesis 2:17). The man cannot fulfill his created purpose alone.

As human creation was the climax of ch Genesis 1:1-31, so human intimacy is the high point of ch Genesis 2:1-25. God’s concern for mutual human support and companionship finds no parallel in ancient Near Eastern literature.

to see what he would call them: Following God’s example (Genesis 1:5, Genesis 1:8, Genesis 1:10), the man chose a name for each of the creatures. In so doing, he was exercising his reign over creation (Genesis 1:26, Genesis 1:28).

Adam recognized the woman as a “helper just right for him” (Genesis 2:20). His celebration of her in poetry and song observed his unity with her, not their distinctions (cp. Genesis 29:14). • Adam declares that “She will be called ‘woman’ (Hebrew ’ishah) because she was taken from ‘man’ (Hebrew ’ish).” He understood the nature of their connection (see Ephesians 5:28-29). Adam had earlier assessed the animals without finding the characteristics he needed in a partner. How different this evaluation is!

Marriage between a man and a woman is not just a human social construct but is rooted in the created order. • a man leaves . . . and is joined: Marriage entails a shift of loyalty from parents to spouse. • the two are united into one: Marriage and its commitments make it the most fundamental covenant relationship observed among humans. Marriage is a powerful image of Israel’s covenant with God (Hosea 2:14-23) and of Christ’s relationship to the church (Ephesians 5:22-32). Marriage is designed as an inseparable, exclusive relationship between a man and a woman. The family unit it creates is the basic building block of human society.

both naked: Prior to the Fall (ch Genesis 3:1-24), nakedness reflected innocence and trust. After the Fall, it denoted vulnerability and shame (see Genesis 9:22-23; Leviticus 18:1-23; Isaiah 47:3). Shame is more than embarrassment; it connotes exploitation and humiliation (see Deuteronomy 28:48; Isaiah 58:7; James 2:15-16).

Genesis describes the deceiver as a serpent, one of the animals God created (see also Genesis 3:14 and study note). He is later identified as Satan, the great enemy of God’s people (Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2). His manipulative language and his disguise as a serpent, the shrewdest of all creatures, show him as a master deceiver. Satan has various methods for opposing God’s people (see 1 Chr 21:1; Zechariah 3:1-2); deception remains among his key strategies (cp. 2 Cor 11:3, 14). The Hebrew term for shrewd (‘arum) can be positive (“prudent,” Proverbs 14:8) or negative (as here; see Job 5:12). It forms a wordplay with “naked” (‘arummim) in Genesis 2:25. Adam and Eve were naked and vulnerable; the serpent was shrewd and cunning. • Probably the serpent asked the woman because the prohibition was given to Adam prior to Eve’s creation (see Genesis 2:16-17). Adam was probably aware of the serpent’s cunning, having assessed and named all the animals before Eve was created (Genesis 2:19-20, Genesis 2:23). • Did God really say? The deceiver began by twisting God’s language to cast doubt on God’s goodness. God’s original prohibition applied to only one tree (Genesis 2:16-17), not to all (any) of them.
The rebellion of the man and the woman shattered their unity and harmony with earth, animals, each other, and God.

The woman attempted to set the record straight; in the process, she belittled the privileges God had given her and her husband in several ways: (1) She reduced God’s “freely eat” (Genesis 2:16) to may eat; (2) she downplayed God’s emphasis on the availability of fruit from every tree but one (Genesis 2:17); (3) she added not touching to God’s prohibition against eating (Genesis 2:17); and (4) she softened the certainty of death (Genesis 2:17).

You won’t die! This is the exact negation of God’s clear and emphatic words: “you are sure to die” (Genesis 2:17). The serpent capitalizes on the woman’s uncertainty by baldly denying the penalty and quickly diverting her attention to the supposed prize—to be like God, knowing both good and evil. The deceiver falsely implies that this would be an unqualified good for them. The term rendered God is Elohim; it can also mean “divine beings” (i.e., God and the angels; e.g., Psalm 29:1; Psalm 89:7).

She saw . . . she wanted: The woman made two grave errors. (1) She assumed the right to decide what was and was not good, though God alone has this right; and (2) she coveted God’s wisdom (see Deuteronomy 5:21). • her husband . . . with her: Although Scripture is clear about the woman’s central role in the Fall (cp. 1 Tim 2:14), the man was clearly present and culpable as well. He comes to center stage in the verses that follow and in biblical theology. The consequence of his sin for the entire human race was immense. The Good News is that in Jesus Christ, the “second Adam,” God has made salvation universally available (Romans 5:12-21).

Shame is opposite to the naked innocence Adam and Eve enjoyed prior to their rebellion (Genesis 2:25). Their relationship with one another and with God was fractured. • sewed fig leaves together: These covered their physical bodies, but not their shame. They could not mend their broken relationships (see also Genesis 3:21 and study note).

When the cool evening breezes were blowing: The Hebrew has traditionally been interpreted as referring to the cool part of the day, most likely the evening. Others think that the language refers to a powerful manifestation of God’s presence (a theophany; see Exodus 19:16-25; 1 Sam 7:10) as a storm. If this view is correct, the man and the woman were hiding from the sound of the Lord appearing in judgment (see 2 Sam 5:24; Psalm 29:1-11). • God put trees in the garden as an environment for humanity to enjoy fellowship with God. Now the man and woman used them to evade the divine presence.

Where are you? The true intent of this rhetorical question is revealed in the man’s answer (Genesis 3:10). The real question was, why are you hiding? (cp. Genesis 4:9-10). • I was afraid because I was naked: Modesty was not the issue. The shame brought on by rebellion drove Adam and his wife to hide. Possibly they also feared punishment (see study note on 3:8).
It was the woman you gave me: Rather than confessing, the man became evasive. He blamed the woman for giving him the fruit and God for giving him the woman.

What have you done? is another rhetorical question that is really an exclamation of horror (cp. Genesis 4:10). • The serpent deceived me: As the man implicated the woman (Genesis 3:12), the woman accused the serpent. The serpent did play a role and would be punished (Genesis 3:14), but that did not release the woman or the man from their guilt.

to the serpent: Though later revelation identifies the deceiver as Satan, it is the created animal who was cursed, like the ground (Genesis 3:17). • Groveling in the dust reflects a posture of humiliation and defeat (Psalm 72:9; Micah 7:17).

The parties were judged in the order of their transgression—serpent, woman, man. Each received a punishment unique to his or her situation, and each had a key relationship altered. God is principled in judgment, not fickle; each punishment is proportionate to the offense.

hostility: The prophet Isaiah envisions the day when the Messiah’s kingdom will restore all of creation to a harmonious state like the Garden of Eden before humans sinned (see Isaiah 11:8). • her offspring (literally her seed): This collective noun can refer to a single descendant or many. The ancient Near Eastern concept of corporate solidarity (e.g., “you and your descendants,” Genesis 28:14) is also behind this description of the ongoing hostility that would exist between humans and snakes. The pattern is set using singular terms (He . . . you). Christian interpreters have traditionally understood this verse as a prophecy of Christ, the seed of Abraham and the culmination of the woman’s seed (Galatians 3:16; Galatians 4:4). • strike: The striking of his heel is a reference to the suffering of God’s servant (see Isaiah 53:1-12), while striking the serpent’s head—a more definitive blow—is ultimately fulfilled in Christ’s death, resurrection, and final victory over Satan (1 Cor 15:55-57; Revelation 12:7-9; Revelation 20:7-10).

Judgment falls on the woman’s unique role of childbearing and on her relationship with her husband. • And you will desire to control your husband, but he will rule over you: The marriage relationship now included an element of antagonism rather than just security and fulfillment. New life in Christ allows for the restoration of a man and a woman’s marriage relationship (Ephesians 5:18-32; cp. Matthew 20:25-28).

God highlighted his original command not to eat the fruit by speaking of eating several times in Genesis 3:17-19. The judgment affected humanity’s ability to get food, and it was proportionate to their offense of eating what had been prohibited. • the ground is cursed: The relationship of the man to the ground (see study note on 2:7) was now antagonistic as judgment fell on his primary role (Genesis 2:5, Genesis 2:15). He must labor and toil to work the ground, but with diminished productivity. Human sin has broad effects on creation (see Genesis 4:12; Genesis 6:7; Leviticus 26:1-46; Deuteronomy 11:13-17, Deuteronomy 11:28; Romans 8:22).

Eve (Hebrew khawah) sounds like a Hebrew term (khayah) that means “to give life.” Following God’s pronouncement of Adam’s impending death (Genesis 3:19), Adam expressed hope by giving Eve a name associated with life. Adam’s naming of Eve in such close proximity to Genesis 3:16 may suggest that the narrator views it as Adam’s first act of ruling over the woman after the Fall (see study note on 2:19-20).
Soon after they were judged for their sin, Adam and Eve were banished from the garden.
God mercifully provided more substantial clothing for Adam and Eve (cp. Genesis 3:7) before expelling them into the harsh environment outside the garden.

like us: The plural probably reflects God’s conversation with his angelic court (see study note on 1:26). • the tree of life . . . live forever! Mercifully, God prevented humankind from eating of the tree of life and having to live forever in a fallen state. Through Jesus Christ, however, eternal life is once again made available (see Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:2, Revelation 22:14, Revelation 22:19).

So the Lord God banished them from the Garden of Eden: Before the Fall, the garden was a sanctuary in which humans could move freely in God’s holy presence. Now their sin required expulsion from that environment. This same principle was behind the laws that restricted an Israelite’s access to God’s presence in the Tabernacle or Temple (e.g., Leviticus 16:1-2; Numbers 5:3).

Cherubim are a class of angelic beings that guard access to God’s presence (Exodus 26:31; Ezekiel 28:14). • east . . . of Eden: In Genesis, movement eastward often implies leaving the presence or blessing of God, whether in judgment (see also Genesis 4:16), self-aggrandizement (Genesis 11:2; Genesis 13:11), or estrangement (Genesis 25:6).

had sexual relations (literally knew): In certain contexts, the Hebrew term meaning “to know” is an idiom for sexual knowledge of another person (Genesis 4:17; Genesis 19:33, Genesis 19:35). It is never used of animals, which mate by instinct. • With the Lord’s help:: Eve fulfilled her God-given role of procreation despite the negative effects of the Fall (see Genesis 3:16, Genesis 3:20). • I have produced: Cain (Hebrew qayin) sounds like a Hebrew term (qanah) that can mean “produce” or “acquire.”
his brother . . . Abel: The name (Hebrew habel) means “breath,” “vapor,” or “meaningless,” anticipating his tragically brief life (cp. Ecclesiastes 1:2).

There was nothing wrong with offering grain to the Lord (Leviticus 2:14; Deuteronomy 26:2-4), but Cain brought only a token gift (some of his crops), whereas God requires the first and best (Exodus 23:16, Exodus 23:19; Exodus 34:22, Exodus 34:26). Cain’s heart attitude made his offering inferior to Abel’s (cp. Hebrews 11:4).

the best portions of the firstborn lambs: Or the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions. Abel was giving God the best animals and the richest parts. Abel’s offering, in contrast to Cain’s, was the best he had to offer. True worship is a costly privilege.

Sin is crouching at the door . . . you must subdue it: Sin is pictured as a vicious animal lying in wait to pounce on Cain (cp. study note on 3:16). Either sin will dominate Cain, or Cain will resist the temptation to sin. There is no neutral ground in that conflict.

The effects of the Fall on human relationships are tragically expressed in the first murder. • The word brother is used seven times in Genesis 4:2-11, highlighting Cain’s fratricide in the face of familial responsibility.

Where is your brother? The questions God asked Cain (Genesis 4:6, Genesis 4:9, Genesis 4:10) recall those that God asked Cain’s parents (Genesis 3:9-13). In both cases, humans put up evasive answers (cp. Genesis 3:12-13). Cain’s answer is shockingly defiant—another clue that the problem with his token offering was the attitude that lay behind it.

What have you done? is more an expression of horror and rebuke than a fact-finding question (cp. Genesis 3:13). • Abel’s blood is personified as a legal witness that cries out against Cain. • from the ground: See study note on 4:11-12.

As with his father (cp. Genesis 3:9-12, Genesis 3:17-19), Cain’s interrogation (Genesis 4:9-10) was followed by God’s verdict. Adam’s sin had already caused the ground to be cursed. Now Cain was cursed and banished from the land he farmed because he had contaminated it with innocent blood. • homeless wanderer: Cain was condemned to ceaseless roving in a land that would provide neither sustenance nor security. The effects of sin were escalating.

For Cain, eviction from the land—the domain of his vocation as a farmer (see Genesis 4:2; cp. Genesis 3:23)—amounted to exile from God’s presence. The Israelites were warned that unfaithfulness to the Sinai covenant would similarly result in eviction from the Promised Land and from God’s presence in the Temple (see, e.g., Leviticus 26:27-32).

Sevenfold punishment was the full weight of justice. Cain complained that his punishment was too great, but the full sentence that would fall on anyone who committed Cain’s crime against him shows how gracious the Lord was to Cain. Cain deserved death (see Genesis 9:5-6). • The mark graciously provided protection following Cain’s judgment (cp. Genesis 3:21).

The name Nod speaks more of Cain’s fate (see Genesis 4:12, Genesis 4:14) than of a specific geographical area (the location is unknown). Cain’s sin denied him rest and a sense of belonging. • Cain’s exile east of Eden is another point of connection with Adam’s story (cp. Genesis 3:24). Cain did not learn from his father’s mistake, so he also suffered estrangement from the ground and exile to the east (see study note on 3:24).

Cain’s wife was probably one of his sisters (Genesis 5:4). Cain’s marriage to his sister would not have caused genetic problems so early in the development of the human gene pool. • Cain was condemned to be a wanderer. Perhaps he founded a city in rebellion against that verdict, seeking to defend himself by enclosing it in walls. Naming it after his son reflects a tendency among those who rebel against God to idolize humanity and its achievements.

These back-to-back genealogies do more than list names for the record. They contrast the ways that human culture spread, some in rebellion against God (Cain, Genesis 4:17-24) and some in obedience to God (Seth, Genesis 4:25–5:32). In Genesis, the history of the rejected branch is generally explained before carrying forward the line that led to Israel. Two points of contrast are especially worth noting: (1) Lamech, the seventh from Adam through the lineage of Cain, is the main focus of the first genealogy. Like his ancestor, Lamech took human life and had to live in constant fear of death as a consequence (Genesis 4:23-24). By contrast, Enoch, the seventh from Adam through the lineage of Seth (see Genesis 4:25–5:32), lived in a way that pleased God and avoided death altogether (Genesis 5:24). (2) Advances in human culture and technology came through Cain’s line (the first city, livestock, shelter, metallurgy, music), but the effects of sin still dominated. No technological advances are mentioned in Seth’s line; instead, people began “to worship the Lord” (Genesis 4:26) and to find “favor with the Lord” (see Genesis 6:8).
the father of: Or the ancestor of, and so throughout the verse. Hebrew genealogies do not necessarily list every single generation.
Marrying two women was contrary to God’s ideal pattern for marriage (Genesis 2:24) and might be another manifestation of the arrogance and rebellion of Cain’s descendants.
Technological advancement masks increasing self-assertion and distance from God (see study note on 4:17–5:32).

Lamech’s chilling taunt shows the further escalation of sin’s effects on humanity. Cain’s line had reached a crescendo of violence with Lamech’s contempt for life. In his arrogance, he put his deed into poetic verse. • punished seventy-seven times! God warned that anyone who tried to kill Cain would experience the full weight of justice (Genesis 4:15). Lamech’s declaration that anyone who harmed him would receive an even more severe penalty is a claim to be accountable to no one, including God.
another son in place of Abel: Cain (Genesis 4:8-16) and Lamech (Genesis 4:19-24) illustrate sin’s consequences; the birth of Seth brought renewed hope. See also study note on 5:1-2.
The story returns to Adam and follows the line of Seth, whose lineage led to Abraham and the Israelite nation.

Enosh means “humankind.” In the Old Testament, the term is often used in poetic texts that emphasize human mortality, frailty, and weakness (e.g., Psalm 144:3, “mere mortals”). Enosh was born at the time when people began to worship the Lord by name (literally call on the name of the Lord). In Genesis, that meant calling on the name of the Lord through sacrifice and prayer (similar Hebrew terminology is found in Genesis 12:8; Genesis 13:4; Genesis 21:33; Genesis 26:25).

written account: Although the previous account (Genesis 2:4–4:26) focused on Adam, Eve, and their first children, it was technically “the account of the . . . heavens and the earth.” Genesis 5:1-32 is a more typical genealogy. • like himself: See Genesis 1:26 and study note.
This is the prologue to the second account in Genesis (Genesis 5:1–6:8; see study note on 2:4); it connects God’s purpose in creation with Seth’s line rather than Cain’s (Genesis 4:17-24).

The genealogies of Genesis go beyond simply recording history. By selective information and by structure, they communicate spiritual truth. The genealogies highlight God’s blessing, authenticate the family heritage of important individuals, and hold the Genesis narrative together by showing familial continuity. Adam’s genealogy through Seth traces ten generations to Noah (see 1 Chr 1:1-4; Luke 3:36-38), with the flood intervening before another ten generations from Noah to Abram. The number ten indicates completeness (ten plagues, Exodus 7:8–11:10; Ten Commandments, Exodus 20:2-17). Noah closed history before the flood, and Abram inaugurated a new era.
male and female . . . “human” (Hebrew ’adam): See Genesis 1:27 and study note. • blessed them: See Genesis 1:28 and study note.
just like him—in his very image: The image and likeness of God (see note on Genesis 1:26) is preserved in human beings despite sin. Adam’s sinful nature was also carried forward (Romans 5:12-14).

he died: Death indeed came to Adam (see Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:18-19) and his descendants (see Romans 5:12-14). Cain’s violence is omitted (see Genesis 4:8, Genesis 4:15, Genesis 4:23-24) and key figures in Seth’s line live in hope (Genesis 5:29).
the father of: Or the ancestor of; Hebrew genealogies do not necessarily list every single generation.

Enoch lived in close fellowship with God (literally Enoch walked with God; also in Genesis 5:24): Enoch’s position as seventh from Adam in the genealogy strikes a contrast with Lamech, the seventh from Adam in the line of Cain (see study note on 4:17–5:32).
Unlike all other sons of Adam, Enoch did not succumb to death; rather, he disappeared, because God took him (cp. 2 Kgs 2:9-12; see also Hebrews 11:5).
969 years: This statement and the numbers given in Genesis 5:25, Genesis 5:28 and Genesis 7:6 mean that Methuselah died in the year of the flood.

As with Enoch (Genesis 5:21-24), the normal genealogical formula is interrupted to highlight important theological information about Noah. Noah sounds like Hebrew nakham, “relief” or “comfort,” and nuakh, “rest.” As the first person born after Adam’s death (see study note on 5:5), Noah prompted his father Lamech to hope that the curse brought on by Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17) might be lifted. See Genesis 8:21; 2 Cor 1:3-7; 2 Thes 2:16-17.

The sons of God have generally been understood as fallen angels (cp. the same Hebrew phrase in Job 1:6; Job 2:1; Job 38:7; Psalm 29:1; Psalm 89:7). This interpretation is prominent in ancient Jewish and Christian literature (e.g., 1 Enoch 6:1–7:6; Justin Martyr, Apology 2.5) and is apparently supported by the New Testament (see 1 Pet 3:18-20; 2 Pet 2:4; Jude 1:6-7). Some interpreters do not believe that God would permit angels to procreate with humans and doubt that the above New Testament texts should be read in this way. Another possibility is that sons of God refers to the righteous descendants of Seth, while the beautiful women were female descendants of Cain’s wicked line. This interpretation is in harmony with Genesis 4:17–5:32 but is weakened by the language of Genesis 6:1-2, which seems to refer to the daughters of humanity in general, not the daughters of Cain specifically. Others believe that sons of God refers to tyrannical human kings (possibly demon-possessed) who took Lamech’s polygamy (Genesis 4:19) to a new height of wickedness by seizing the daughters of the righteous. Language reminiscent of Genesis 3:6 (saw . . . took) shows the rebellious nature of this act.
Human wickedness reached a climax, prompting God to send the flood to destroy all living things. A glimmer of hope appears in God’s favor toward Noah (Genesis 6:8).

will not put up with: Many think that this is an announcement of God’s decision to withdraw the restraining influence of his Spirit from human society and allow human wickedness to run its full course. Others think it means that God would withdraw his life-giving breath from humans at an earlier age (ruakh, the Hebrew term for “spirit,” can also mean “breath”; see Genesis 6:17; Genesis 7:22; see also Psalm 104:29-30). • normal lifespan will be no more than 120 years (literally his days will be 120 years): It is possible that this was a new restriction on the number of years individuals would generally be allowed to live (so the NLT). However, for generations after the flood, humans lived well beyond 120 years (see, e.g., Genesis 11:10-26). An alternative interpretation sees this as a 120-year grace period before the arrival of the flood (see Jonah 3:4; Matthew 24:37-38; 1 Pet 3:20; 2 Pet 2:5).

giant Nephilites (Hebrew nepilim): The term may mean “fallen ones.” The context implies that they were the offspring of the “sons of God” and would be destroyed in the flood. Numbers 13:31-33 uses the same term to describe other giants who were hostile toward God’s people and would also be destroyed (see also Deuteronomy 2:11, which connects the Anakite nepilim with another group called the repa’im).

everything they thought or imagined (literally every intention of the thoughts of their hearts): In the Old Testament, the heart is the core of volition, thought, and morality (see Proverbs 4:23). Wicked actions stem from a corrupt inner life. • consistently and totally evil: Strong language captures the pervasiveness, depth, and persistence of human wickedness. Human nature continued to be corrupt even after the flood (see Genesis 8:21).

the Lord was sorry: The extent of human wickedness made the Lord regret having created them (see also Genesis 6:7; cp. 1 Sam 15:11, 35). • It broke his heart: The evil in humanity’s heart (Genesis 6:5) pained God greatly. Sending the flood was a heart-wrenching act on God’s part.

wipe . . . from the . . . earth: As Adam and Eve were banished from the garden-sanctuary (Genesis 3:23), all of humankind would be expunged from God’s good creation. • every living thing: Human sin had so corrupted the earth that judgment fell on the animals and birds over which they had dominion (see Genesis 1:28 and study note). The special role of humans in the created order (Genesis 1:28-30) means that nature is affected by human moral choices (see Genesis 8:1; Job 38:41; Hosea 4:3; Romans 8:19-22).
Noah and his godly life stand in stark contrast to the sinfulness of the rest of the people.

the account: See study note on 2:4 • a righteous man, the only blameless person: The text does not claim that Noah was without sin (see Romans 5:12-14). Noah’s righteousness and blamelessness came about because he walked in close fellowship with God. See also Genesis 7:1; Genesis 17:1; Hebrews 11:7.
See Genesis 6:5-7. • violence (Hebrew khamas): Murder had especially corrupted the line of Cain (Genesis 4:8, Genesis 23:1–24:67).

The large boat (traditionally rendered ark) was a long rectangular barge designed for survival, not for navigation. The Hebrew word tebah is used again only of the basket in which the baby Moses was floated on the Nile (Exodus 2:3, Exodus 2:5). • cypress wood: It is not clear what kind of wood this was. It was possibly from a conifer, such as cypress.
This floating barge displaced around 43,300 tons of water.

An 18-inch opening below the roof encircled the boat, providing light and air. • Noah was to build a door and God would close it (Genesis 7:16). God was the captain of this peculiar boat with no sail or rudder. God also brought the animals to Noah (Genesis 6:20).

cover the earth with a flood: Some propose that the flood might only have covered the ancient Near East as it was known to Noah or Moses. However, the flood’s stated purpose—to destroy every living thing that breathes (see also Genesis 6:7, Genesis 6:11-13; Genesis 7:1, Genesis 7:4, Genesis 7:18-23; Genesis 8:21)—and its effect of undoing creation (see study notes on 1:9-10; 7:11-12) suggest that the flood covered the entire planet (see also 1 Pet 3:20; 2 Pet 2:5; 3:6).
This first explicit mention of a covenant in the Bible refers to the unilateral pact that God made with humankind and the world after the flood (see Genesis 9:9, Genesis 9:11, Genesis 9:14-17).
God’s instructions to Noah repeat the language of creation (every kind, cp. Genesis 1:24). • a male and a female: These animals would procreate and repopulate the earth after the flood.

of each animal I have approved: In addition to the animals that were to repopulate the earth, these “clean” animals were for food and for Noah’s sacrifice after the flood (Genesis 8:20-21). This passage does not use the precise technical language that is found in the regulations concerning “clean” and “unclean” given to Israel at Sinai (see Leviticus 11:1-47; Deuteronomy 14:3-12), but the underlying concept is the same (perhaps God revealed it directly to Noah).
The number forty is often associated with affliction, trial, or punishment (see Exodus 16:35; Judges 13:1; 1 Kgs 19:8; Ezekiel 4:6; Jonah 3:4; Matthew 4:2; Acts 1:3).
covered the earth: See study note on 6:17.
See study note on 7:2.

on the seventeenth day of the second month: Such information gives the flood account a certain solemnity; it reminds readers that this was a true historical event. • underground waters: See Genesis 2:6. • rain fell: The flood undid the boundaries established on the second and third days of creation (Genesis 1:6-13). Elsewhere, the Bible describes God’s judgment as an undoing of creation (see Jeremiah 4:23-26; Amos 7:4). • forty days and forty nights: See study note on 7:4.
the Lord closed the door: The sovereign Judge took responsibility for the annihilation of all outside the boat and the protection of those within (see also Genesis 6:16 and study note).

floodwaters grew deeper (literally waters multiplied): The same word used for the proliferation of humans and animals during creation (see Genesis 1:22, Genesis 1:28) is now used ironically of the water that would annihilate them. • covering the ground: The Hebrew word translated “ground” or “earth” is mentioned eight times in eight verses (Genesis 7:17-24). The earth is the domain that humankind had polluted and that was now the object of a cleansing deluge.
Everything that . . . lived: See study note on 6:17.

God remembered: This structural and theological center of the flood story does not mean that God had at any point forgotten Noah. This is covenant language reflecting God’s faithfulness to his promise to ensure the safety of his covenant partner (cp. Genesis 6:18; Genesis 9:15-16; Exodus 2:24; Leviticus 26:42, Leviticus 26:45). • wind: The same word is translated “Spirit” in Genesis 1:2. This and other parallels (see Genesis 9:1-2) suggest that the restoration of the earth after the flood was effectively a new creation.
underground waters . . . torrential rains: See study note on 7:11-12.

The mountains of Ararat might be in the region of Ararat (Urartu) southeast of the Black Sea near Lake Van, which touches parts of eastern Turkey, Armenia, and Iran. There is a Mount Ararat (Agri Dag) in Turkey, but this verse only identifies the region, not a specific mountain.
the waters continued to go down: Another parallel with the creation week (see Genesis 1:9) suggests that the earth’s restoration was effectively a new creation (see study note on 8:1).

The raven is the largest member of the crow family, and was among Noah’s unclean animals (Leviticus 11:15; Deuteronomy 14:14). As a scavenger and carrion eater, it was able to sustain itself without returning to the boat.
Unlike the raven (Genesis 8:7), the dove feeds on vegetation. Since olive trees are not tall, Noah could tell that the water was almost gone.
On the first day of the new year, ten and a half months after the flood began: This was two months after the peaks of the mountains first became visible (Genesis 8:5).

the earth was dry! This special word for dry land is uniquely used in connection with the sea to portray God’s sovereignty over both domains (see Genesis 1:9-10; Exodus 14:22, Exodus 14:29; Psalm 95:5; Jonah 1:9).
be fruitful and multiply: See Genesis 9:1.

This first mention of an altar in the Bible shows Noah’s gratitude for having passed through the judgment. • sacrificed as burnt offerings: The same wording is used of the whole burnt offering in Leviticus (Leviticus 1:3-9); however, it can refer to any offering that is burned. Noah gave this offering to thank and worship God, who had delivered him and his family from the flood.

pleased with the aroma of the sacrifice (literally smelled the sweet aroma): The narrator uses anthropomorphic language (i.e., he describes God’s activity in human terms) to show God’s acceptance of Noah’s offering (see also Exodus 29:18; Leviticus 1:9; Numbers 15:3). The common ancient Near Eastern notion that the gods ate the sacrifices offered to them is notably absent. • to himself (literally in his heart): The phrase echoes “broke his heart” (Genesis 6:6), just as think or imagine echoes “everything they thought or imagined” (Genesis 6:5). God’s commitment to a new order replaced his grief over the old. • I will never again curse . . . destroy: The old curse was not lifted (Genesis 5:29), but God promised not to add to it, thus establishing new limits for life in a disordered world (cp. Isaiah 54:9). The flood was to stop violence, not to reform the human heart (Genesis 6:5). Humankind’s bent toward evil would be contained to some degree through accountability to a new law (Genesis 9:5-6).
God’s promise to sustain the rhythm of the seasons reaffirmed the created order (Genesis 1:14; see also Jeremiah 33:20; Zechariah 14:7).
Be fruitful and multiply: The blessing and mandate first given to Adam (Genesis 1:28) are now reissued to Noah, the “Adam” of the newly cleansed world in need of repopulation.

God’s first post-flood speech opens and closes with blessing (Genesis 9:1, Genesis 9:7). In it, human and animal relationships are again defined, with some modification of the original created order. The sanctity of life is given special focus.

There are two modifications to the original created order. (1) Previously, humans reigned over the animals (Genesis 1:28), but now animals would live in terror of humans (similar military language is found in Exodus 23:27-31; Deuteronomy 11:25; Deuteronomy 31:8). (2) The animals’ terror was related to a change in human diet. Humans were now permitted to eat the meat of animals to supplement their subsistence on grains, fruits, and vegetables (Genesis 1:29).

A key restriction is imposed. Since blood was identified with life, it had to be drained from a slain animal before its meat could be eaten (see Leviticus 3:17; Leviticus 7:26-27; Leviticus 17:10-14; Deuteronomy 12:16, Deuteronomy 12:23). The law of Moses prohibited eating animals that died naturally, since their blood had not been drained (Deuteronomy 14:21). God provided animal blood to atone for human sin (Leviticus 17:11; Hebrews 9:22).

Violence, including murder, was a major factor in bringing about God’s judgment of the flood (Genesis 4:8; Genesis 6:11, Genesis 6:13). At this new beginning for humans, God affirmed the sanctity of human life and established a system of retributive justice for the taking of human life (see also Psalm 9:12; “Retribution” Theme Note). The function of law is to restrain human wickedness and preserve moral order. This law was further developed in the law of Moses (Exodus 21:12-14; Leviticus 24:17-22; Numbers 35:16-34; Deuteronomy 17:6-7; Deuteronomy 19:15).

For God made human beings in his own image: The death penalty has a theological basis. God’s image gives humans a unique status and authority within creation (Genesis 1:26-28). Since murder destroys a person made in God’s image, the ultimate penalty must be imposed on a murderer. See also Exodus 21:23-25. We are not to pursue personal revenge (Romans 12:17-19) but are to uphold the justice of the “governing authorities” that God has established (Romans 13:1-7).
Now be fruitful and multiply, and repopulate (literally swarm and fill): In contrast to those who would destroy human life (Genesis 9:5-6), God’s desire is that human life should abound and flourish.
God’s second post-flood speech conveys his promise and plan for preserving creation.
God had promised this covenant before the flood (Genesis 6:18). Its scope extends beyond humanity to include the earth and all animals.
This promise does not prohibit worldwide judgment, but it restricts the means by which God will do it (see 2 Pet 3:4-13).
In the Bible, covenants are frequently confirmed by some sort of sign (e.g., Genesis 17:11; Exodus 31:13, Exodus 31:17; Luke 22:20).

God brought cataclysmic judgment through the rainstorm; now, the rainbow, a meteorological phenomenon associated with the rainstorm, would be an image of peace for all the earth (see Genesis 9:17). • The same Hebrew term denotes both “rainbow” and “bow.” Since God is sometimes pictured as a warrior who shoots arrows of judgment (see Deuteronomy 32:42; Psalm 7:12; Psalm 18:13-14; Habakkuk 3:9-11), some think that the imagery in Genesis 9:13-17 is of the Divine Warrior hanging up his bow of judgment.

Ham is the father of Canaan: See also Genesis 9:20-27; Genesis 10:6-20. The text emphasizes Canaan’s ancestral connection to Ham to show that the Canaanite identity was inseparably linked to Ham’s shameful behavior (Genesis 9:20-27). The citizens of both Egypt (from which Israel escaped slavery) and Canaan (to which Israel was headed) were Ham’s descendants (Genesis 10:6; see Leviticus 18:3, Leviticus 18:24-26; Psalm 105:23, Psalm 105:27; Psalm 106:22). Later stories in Genesis emphasize the immoral climate of both Egypt (Genesis 12:10-20) and Canaan (Genesis 34:1-31; Genesis 38:1-30). See Genesis 9:20-27 and Genesis 10:6-20.

The story of Noah begins with him walking in righteousness and obeying the Lord (Genesis 6:9), but it ends with him lying drunk and naked in his tent and then delivering a curse on Canaan. Even after the great flood, the human race exhibited some of the same sinful characteristics that warranted the judgment in the first place. Special attention is given to the cursed origin of the Canaanites, the corrupt and idolatrous people Israel would later displace from the Promised Land (see also Genesis 15:16 and study note; Leviticus 18:3; Leviticus 20:23).

wine . . . became drunk: Wine is a gift from God (Deuteronomy 14:26; Psalm 104:15; Isaiah 55:1; see Luke 22:14-20; John 2:1-11). Scripture is clear, however, that excessive consumption of alcohol is a perilous sin (Proverbs 23:20-21, Proverbs 23:29-35; 1 Cor 6:10).

the father of Canaan: See study note on 9:18. • Ham’s behavior was shameful. He gazed upon his naked father and, rather than covering him and keeping the matter secret, robbed him of his dignity by announcing it to his brothers (see Exodus 21:15, Exodus 21:17; Lamentations 4:21; Habakkuk 2:15). An ancient Near Eastern tale says that a son is expected to come to his father’s aid when he is drunk (Tale of Aqhat; cp. Isaiah 51:17-18). Ham’s neglect of familial duty explains why Noah praised Shem and Japheth but cursed Ham (Genesis 9:24-27).
Then he cursed Canaan: Noah foresaw Ham’s actions as morally representative of Ham’s descendants through Canaan.
Noah refers to God as the Lord, who formed the covenant with Israel. Shem was the privileged forefather of the Israelites (see Genesis 10:21-32).
May Japheth share the prosperity of Shem: Japheth’s descendants would live among Shem’s descendants and share Shem’s prosperity (cp. Romans 11:17-18).
Many children were born . . . after the great flood: This fulfilled the renewed creation mandate (Genesis 9:1, Genesis 9:9; cp. Genesis 1:28).

The fifth account (Genesis 10:1) in Genesis (see study note on 2:4) unites the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:2-32) and the Babel story (Genesis 11:1-9) around the theme of scattering the nations (Genesis 10:5, Genesis 10:18; Genesis 11:4, Genesis 11:8-9). The Table of Nations precedes the Babel story even though the Babel incident caused the geopolitical situation reflected in the Table of Nations. By reversing the order, Genesis links the repopulation of the earth with the blessing conferred upon Noah and his sons (see Genesis 9:1 and study note) and shows that Abram’s call (Genesis 12:1-3) was God’s solution to the problem of human estrangement from God as reflected in the Babel story (Genesis 11:1-9).

The seven sons of Japheth settled in the region of Anatolia (the western plateau lands of Turkey) and spoke Indo-European languages. • Gomer was the ancestor of the later Cimmerians who lived north of the Black Sea. • Magog was probably the ancestor of those who settled in the region of Lydia (see Ezekiel 38:2). • The descendants of Madai were the later Medes of northwest Iran (see 2 Kgs 17:6; Jeremiah 51:11; Daniel 5:28). • The descendants of Javan were the later Ionian Greeks. • The descendants of Tubal and Meshech were sometimes allies in battle (Ezekiel 38:2). Both were possibly from the coastal regions of Anatolia (see Ezekiel 27:13). • The descendants of Tiras possibly became the Thracians that lived near the Aegean Sea.

This section describes the ancestral origin of the nations of the ancient Near East. Ham was at the center (Genesis 10:6-20), while the descendants of Japheth and Shem spread out to the surrounding regions of Greece, Crete, Asia Minor, Mesopotamia, Madai, the Arabian peninsula, and northeast Africa. The list selectively highlights nations relevant to Israel. The total of seventy (seven times ten) names indicates completeness (see Genesis 46:27; Deuteronomy 32:8) and symbolizes the totality of the world, which would later be blessed by the descendants of Abraham (Genesis 18:18). • Although Shem is mentioned first in Genesis 10:1, he is addressed last in the Table because of his connection to Abram (Genesis 10:21-31; Genesis 11:10-32; Genesis 12:1). Although God established the boundaries of all nations (see Deuteronomy 32:8; Amos 9:7; Acts 17:26), Israel was his special creation—a microcosm of seventy people (Genesis 46:27) called to be a blessing to a world of seventy nations (see Genesis 12:3).

The descendants of Gomer came from near the Upper Euphrates region north of the Black Sea (cp. Ezekiel 38:1-9). • The descendants of Ashkenaz were the later Scythians who inhabited the region between the Black and Caspian Seas. • Riphath is near Carchemish. • The descendants of Togarmah are associated with Til-garimmu, the capital of Kammanu in modern Armenia (see Ezekiel 38:6).

Elishah is probably Cyprus. • Tarshish is possibly southwest Spain (see study note on Jon 1:3). • The Kittim were inhabitants of southern Cyprus. • The Rodanim were inhabitants of the island of Rhodes, later a territory of Greece.

seafaring peoples . . . various lands: They settled around the Mediterranean and on various islands. • language: This occurred after the Tower of Babel episode (Genesis 11:1-9; see study note on 10:1–11:9).

The peoples descended from Ham’s four sons (Egyptians, Babylonians, Assyrians, Canaanites) were Israel’s most hostile neighbors. • Cush was possibly in Ethiopia or ancient Nubia (northern Sudan). • Mizraim was the ancient name for Egypt (Genesis 50:11). • Put was in Libya. • Canaan encompassed southern Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine west of the Jordan River. In Moses’ time, Egypt and Canaan were provinces of the same empire. Ham’s descendants were excluded from the blessing of Shem’s line (Genesis 9:20-28).

The sons of Cush and Raamah together total seven. • Seba was in northern Africa (see Isaiah 43:3; Isaiah 45:14). • Havilah was in southwest Arabia. • Sabtah was in southern Arabia, in ancient Hadramaut, near the Persian Gulf. • Raamah was in southwest Arabia near Najran. • Sabteca was in ancient Samudake near the Persian Gulf. • Sheba was a kingdom in southwest Arabia with commercial colonies (see 1 Kgs 10:1-29). • Dedan was in northern Arabia.
Special attention is given to the early history of Babylonia and Assyria, the Mesopotamian empires that would conquer and exile Israel and Judah.

Nimrod attained great fame by conquest and terror; his empire extended from Babylonia in the south to Assyria in the north (Genesis 10:10-12). • the greatest hunter in the world: Assyrian monarchs glorified their own power, often depicting themselves as valiant hunter-conquerors.

Babylonia is the area surrounding the Tigris and Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia. This kingdom eventually reached into northern Mesopotamia (Assyria). • Of the cities mentioned, Babylon is most important because of its role in building the Tower of Babel (see Genesis 11:4 and study note). • Erech was ancient Uruk and is now Warka in southern Iraq (see Ezra 4:9-10). • Akkad was the ancient Agade north of Babylon, home of the famous ruler Sargon (2370–2295 BC). • The location of Calneh is uncertain, though it is presumably one of Nimrod’s cities located north of Aram-naharaim in southern Mesopotamia (cp. Amos 6:2). • building . . . Nineveh: Like Cain, Nimrod built cities (see Genesis 4:17 and comments). Nineveh was an ancient Assyrian city on the east bank of the Tigris River in northern Iraq. • Rehoboth-ir was a daughter-city of Nineveh or was located nearby. • Calah is modern Tell Nimrud, south of Nineveh. • Resen is possibly modern Selamiyeh, northwest of Tell Nimrud.

The Ludites were Lydian tribes west of the Nile delta. • The identity of the Anamites is uncertain. They were possibly Egyptians near Cyrene, west of Egypt. • The Lehabites were possibly a Libyan tribe. • The Naphtuhites inhabited northern Egypt. • The Pathrusites inhabited southern Egypt. • The Casluhites possibly inhabited an Egyptian district also known as Cyrenaica. • The Caphtorites were Cretans (see Jeremiah 47:4; Amos 9:7). • The Philistines from Crete were sea people who lived intermittently in southwest Canaan during the period of the Exodus and later (Exodus 13:17; Amos 9:7). They were among Israel’s most troublesome enemies during the early monarchy (see 1–2 Samuel).

Sidon settled in Phoenicia, north of Canaan. • Hittites: The Hittites in Genesis were a coalition of cities within Canaan (see Genesis 26:34-35; Genesis 27:46; Ezekiel 16:3). They were probably not the same as the Hittites of Anatolia (Asia Minor), whose empire was one of the great empires of antiquity during the patriarchal period. • The Jebusites were ancient inhabitants of Jerusalem (Joshua 15:63; Judges 19:10-11; 2 Sam 5:6-9). • The Amorites lived throughout the mountains of Palestine in Canaan (see Genesis 15:16; Genesis 48:22; Numbers 13:29; Deuteronomy 3:8; Joshua 10:5; Judges 1:35; Judges 10:8; Ezekiel 16:3). • Little is known of the Girgashites, a Canaanite tribe (Genesis 15:21; Deuteronomy 7:1; Joshua 3:10). • The Hivites were an uncircumcised Canaanite tribe (Genesis 34:2, Genesis 34:13-24; Joshua 9:1, Joshua 9:7; Joshua 11:3; Judges 3:3; 2 Sam 24:7). • The Arkites resided in Tell ’Arqa in Lebanon. • The Sinites formed a city-state and inhabited Phoenicia. • The Arvadites inhabited Ruad in northern Phoenicia, near the El Kebir River. They were known for shipping (cp. Ezekiel 27:8). • The Zemarites inhabited Sumur (modern Sumra), north of Arka on the Phoenician coast. • The Hamathites founded what is now Hama on the Orontes River, the northern boundary of Canaan (see Numbers 34:8; Joshua 13:5; 2 Sam 8:9-10; 1 Kgs 8:65; 2 Kgs 14:25-28).

The territory of Canaan is specifically marked off because it would be taken from its inhabitants and given to Israel (see Genesis 15:18; Numbers 34:2-12; Ezekiel 47:15-20; Ezekiel 48:1-28). • An ancient north-south seacoast highway (the Via Maris) extended from Sidon . . . to Gerar, connecting Egypt to Mesopotamia. • Modern Gaza is 11 miles northwest of Gerar. • Sodom and Gomorrah were cities on the border of the land southeast of the Dead Sea. • Admah and Zeboiim are mentioned 15 times in connection with Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 14:2, Genesis 14:8; Deuteronomy 29:23; see Hosea 11:8). All four cities were destroyed by God to cleanse the land (see Genesis 19:1-38). • Lasha was possibly in the northern region of the Dead Sea.

Shem, the older brother of Japheth, was the father of the Semitic peoples. The descendants listed represent countries east of Israel (modern Iraq, Iran, and Syria). The narrator lists these locations within Mesopotamia since Abram, the father of Israel, originated from this area (see Genesis 11:27-32). • Eber receives special attention because of his connection with Abram (see study note on 10:24).

The descendants of Elam lived in the region of modern southwestern Iran (see Genesis 14:1, Genesis 14:9; Ezra 4:9; Isaiah 11:11). • The descendants of Asshur were later Assyrians who lived under Nimrod’s jurisdiction (see Genesis 10:11). Sumerians descended from Ham were ousted by Mesopotamian Semites. • Arphaxad possibly settled northeast of Nineveh; his descendants are further described in Genesis 11:12-26. • Lud was near the Tigris River; its people were related to the Lydians (see Genesis 10:13). • Aram was a kingdom of tribes that lived in the Mesopotamian plains.

The patriarchs later interacted with the descendants of Aram (see Genesis 25:20; Genesis 31:20; Deuteronomy 26:5). • Uz was the chief Aramean tribe, possibly located northeast of the Jordan; it was Job’s home (see Job 1:1; see also Lamentations 4:21). • Hul is unknown. He possibly founded Armenia. • Gether is unknown; he was possibly the founder of the Syrians. • Mash might be associated with Mount Masus in northern Mesopotamia or with a part of the Lebanon Mountains.

Shelah is unknown, but may be short for Methushelah (cp. Genesis 38:5, Genesis 38:11). • Eber was the ancestor of Abram the Hebrew (Genesis 11:10-26); his name is at the root of the term “Hebrew” (see Genesis 14:13; Genesis 39:14; Genesis 40:15; Genesis 41:12; Exodus 2:11; Exodus 3:18).

Peleg means division, anticipating the separation of people into language groups after Babel (Genesis 11:1-9). Peleg’s line led to Abram (see Genesis 11:16-26). • Joktan was the ancestor of the southern Arabian tribes. The Ishmaelite tribes were in northern Arabia (see Genesis 25:13-16).

Almodad was an ancestor, region, or tribe in modern Yemen. • Sheleph was a tribe of Yemen. • Hazarmaveth was related to Hadramaut in southern Arabia. • Jerah is unknown, but was possibly associated with Mount Barach. • Hadoram was an Arabian tribe. • Uzal was Sana’a, an old capital of Yemen in pre-Islamic times. • Diklah was a southern Arabian oasis in Mina. • Obal was between Hodeida and Sana’a in southwest Arabia. • Abimael was a Sabaean. • Sheba was in southern Arabia (see Genesis 10:7). • Ophir was a region of southern Arabia between Sheba and Havilah; it was a source of gold (Isaiah 13:12). • Havilah: See Genesis 10:7. • Jobab was possibly Jobebitai in southern Arabia.

There were fourteen sons of Shem by Eber through Joktan. The placement of the Babel story between the lines of Joktan and Peleg ties Joktan to the judgment of the Babel story (Genesis 11:1-9) and ties Peleg to Abram (Genesis 11:27–12:1).
Mesha was a region in northern Arabia, south of Hadramaut. • Sephar is identified with Isfar, south of Hadramaut in Yemen.

At one time: The events described in Genesis 11:1-9 led to the scattering of nations that is reflected in the genealogies of Genesis 10:2-30. The reversal of order has a theological purpose (see study note on 10:1–11:9).

The story of the unfinished tower carries forward themes of language and solidarity from the Table of Nations (ch Genesis 10:1-32). The builders’ desire for autonomy recalls the rebellion in Eden (ch Genesis 3:1-24) and establishes the need for Abram’s redemptive faith in the midst of international disorder (ch Genesis 12:1-20). The scattering of the nations anticipates the warning to Israel that idolatry would result in their being scattered and their cities devastated (see Leviticus 26:33; Numbers 10:35; Deuteronomy 4:27; Deuteronomy 28:64; Deuteronomy 30:3). Chronologically, the story is a flashback that explains the rise of the nations during Peleg’s time (see Genesis 10:25).

migrated to the east: See study note on 3:24. • Babylonia was located in southern Mesopotamia, the region of Nimrod’s later empire and city-building campaign (see Genesis 10:10; Isaiah 11:11; Daniel 1:2; Zechariah 5:11).

Stone was plentiful in Canaan; in Mesopotamia, stone was scarce and brick technology was developed. • Tar was made from bitumen, a natural, cement-like, waterproof asphalt (see Genesis 6:14; Exodus 2:3).

Far from the original garden (Genesis 2:15), the first cities of Genesis represent arrogance (Genesis 4:17), tyranny (Genesis 10:8-12), and wickedness (Genesis 18:20-21). The city on the Babylonian plain was a magnet for human pride and idolatry. • a tower that reaches into the sky: This was probably a temple-tower (a ziggurat). Common in ancient Babylonian urban culture, ziggurats were regarded as sacred mountains by which deities descended to earth (Jacob’s dream in Genesis 28:12 possibly reflects this idea). • This will make us famous (literally let us make a name for ourselves): The tower builders sought fame through idolatrous ambition. God promised to give Abram a famous name because of his humble obedience (Genesis 12:2).

came down: The tower was a human attempt to ascend to God’s realm (see Deuteronomy 26:15; Psalm 2:4; Psalm 103:19; Psalm 115:16). The folly of that attempt was exposed by God’s “coming down” to see their feeble efforts.
If left unchecked, the tower builders’ solidarity and ambition would allow human wickedness to flourish in unimaginable ways.

Come, let’s go down: God addresses his angelic court (see Genesis 1:26; Genesis 3:22; and study notes). • won’t be able to understand each other: Their inability to communicate would curtail their unified sinful ambition. The God-honoring unity of language on the day of Pentecost was a symbolic reversal of the Babel dispersion (Acts 2:5-13; see Zephaniah 3:9).

the Lord scattered them: Similarly, Adam and Eve’s punishment for grasping at autonomy and Cain’s punishment for murder involved banishment and dispersion (Genesis 3:23; Genesis 4:12, Genesis 4:14; Genesis 9:19; Genesis 10:5, Genesis 10:25, Genesis 10:32).

Babel: The Babylonians viewed their city as the residence or gateway of the gods. The pun that concludes this account accurately reveals Babylon’s spiritual confusion. Babylon achieved prominence under Nimrod (Genesis 10:10) and in later biblical history (see 2 Kgs 25:1-30). Its role as an epicenter of arrogance and idolatry make it a fitting image for the anti-God forces associated with the end of time (e.g., Revelation 14:8; Revelation 16:19; Revelation 18:2). • The tower builders had centralized to ascend into God’s realm (Genesis 11:3-4). God descended and scattered them all over the world to frustrate their idolatrous ambition.

This account of Shem’s family resumes the line of Shem from Genesis 10:21-32, now with special focus on the line leading to Abram. Only Abram and Israel are heirs to Shem’s God (see Genesis 9:26-27; Deuteronomy 32:8-9). The Babel story vividly repudiates the culture that Abram was called to abandon (Genesis 12:1; Genesis 24:6-7). Together with the account of Terah’s descendants (Genesis 11:27-32), this second account of Shem’s line forms a bridge from the universal history of chs Genesis 1:1–11:32 to the national history of Israel that begins in ch Genesis 12:1-20. Abram is the remnant from Babel’s confused world. God called him as an act of grace whereby the fractured world of Babel would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). • the father of: Or the ancestor of; Hebrew genealogies do not necessarily list every single generation.
Peleg: See study note on 10:25.
Nahor was the grandfather of Laban, whose daughters later became Jacob’s wives (chs Genesis 29:1–31:55). • Lot: See “Lot” Profile.

This brief section provides a complete summary of Terah’s life and accounts for his other sons and their marriages; it also introduces Lot, Abram’s nephew, who later played a prominent role. The ancestors, including Terah and his family, were idolatrous, worshiping other gods in Mesopotamia (Joshua 24:2).

This is the account (Hebrew toledoth; see study note on 2:4) of Terah’s family: What follows in Genesis 11:28–25:11 are the particulars about the family descended from Terah, notably about Abraham and God’s covenant with him, and about Isaac, the child of promise, who carried forward the line and the blessing to the next generation.

The call of Abram occurred in Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 15:7; Acts 7:2-4), the main city of Sumer in Mesopotamia near the mouth of the Persian Gulf. The family had moved there perhaps generations before the call. Their ancestral home (“native country,” Genesis 12:1) was apparently near Haran, in the region of the descendants of Shem (Genesis 11:10-26); thus they settled there when they left Ur (Genesis 11:31) and were later described as “Arameans” (Deuteronomy 26:5). • land of his birth: The same Hebrew phrase is repeated in Genesis 12:1 (“native country”), making Ur, not Haran, the location of Abram’s call (see Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:7; Acts 7:2).

Sarai means “princess” in Hebrew. No mention is made of Sarai’s parentage, perhaps to add suspense to the Abimelech story, which reveals that she was Abram’s half sister (Genesis 20:9-12). Later, the law prohibited such a marriage (Leviticus 18:9; Leviticus 20:17; Deuteronomy 27:22). • Nahor’s wife was Milcah: Milcah was Haran’s daughter and Nahor’s niece (see Genesis 11:29). Her son Bethuel was the father of Rebekah, the wife of Abram’s son Isaac (Genesis 24:10, Genesis 24:15, Genesis 24:24). The name Milcah is related to the Hebrew word meaning “queen.” In Akkadian, it is a title of the goddess Ishtar, the moon-god’s daughter. Terah’s name is related to the word for “moon” in Hebrew; his whole family appears to have worshiped Sin, the moon-god (see Joshua 24:14).

Sarai, Rebekah (Genesis 25:21), and Rachel (Genesis 29:31) all suffered infertility. Sarai’s situation in particular highlights the paradox between the apparent reality and God’s promise to give many descendants (Genesis 12:2). The Israelite nation’s origin from barren women fixes its identity in the sovereignty of God, who miraculously gives children to barren women (see also 1 Sam 1:2; 2:5; Psalm 113:9; Isaiah 54:1).

Terah took: The text is clear that Abram’s departure from Ur was prompted by God’s calling (see study note on 11:28), but the event is described from Terah’s perspective, in keeping with the patriarchy of ancient Near Eastern culture. This cultural deference to the oldest male is evidently why Abram did not continue on to Canaan by himself at this time (see Acts 7:2-4). • Haran was 550 miles northwest of Ur, near the Syrian-Turkish border. Despite the similar name, there is no connection with Terah’s son Haran, who had died in Ur (Genesis 11:28). • Haran means “caravan.” Ancient commercial routes converged there, making it a key site for trade. • Haran was also well known for the moon worship to which Terah’s family was apparently devoted (see study note on 11:29).
Abram knew that he should leave, but he did not know where he was going. Obedience required faith.
These verses are structured around two commands to Abram: Leave and be a blessing (see study note on 12:2). Each directive is followed by three promises conditioned upon obedience.

Through Abram’s faith and family, God began restoring the blessing. God called Abram from a pagan world to begin a new nation; his promises to Abram later became a covenant (ch Genesis 15:1-21). • God’s call to Abram later helped convince the Israelites to leave Egypt and go to the land God promised to Abram. It also reminded the Babylonian exiles of their need to return to their own land (e.g., Isaiah 51:1-23).

make you famous (literally make your name great): Abram received the fame sought by the builders of Babel (see Genesis 11:4 and study note). • and you will be a blessing (or so that you will be a blessing): This clause is a command in Hebrew, but it is also a promise conditioned upon Abram’s obedience to God’s command (Genesis 12:1): “Go . . . so that you will be a blessing. Be a blessing, so that I can bless and curse others.”

Based on Abram’s obedience to the command to be a blessing (Genesis 12:2), God gave him three more promises. • those who treat you with contempt: People who disregarded Abram and his covenant were rejecting God’s choice and plan. • All the families on earth will be blessed: By faith, they could participate in the covenant God was making with Abram. The blessing spread to the whole world through Abraham, Israel, the covenants, the prophets, Scripture, and the Messiah (Galatians 3:8, Galatians 3:16; cp. Romans 9:4-5).

Abram was middle-aged, settled, prosperous, aristocratic, and polytheistic (see study note on 11:27-32). When the Lord spoke to him (Genesis 12:1-3), he obediently left his old ways in Ur to follow God’s plan. Since Abram responded in faith, God’s promises (Genesis 12:2-3) could be confirmed in a binding covenant (Genesis 15:8-21).
Abram’s obedience to God’s call corresponded to God’s commands (see study note on 12:1-3). He journeyed to Canaan (Genesis 12:4-6) and became a blessing (Genesis 12:5-9).

The people (Hebrew hannepesh, “the lives”) he had taken into his household were probably converts; Abram first became a blessing by influencing people in his household to join him in following the Lord.

The oak of Moreh was apparently a Canaanite shrine; fertile groves of trees were sacred to the Canaanites (cp. Isaiah 1:29), and Moreh means “teacher.” Abram proclaimed (Luther: “preached”) the Lord’s name beside a pagan place of worship and instruction (Genesis 12:8). • Abram continued to be a blessing when he built an altar to worship God at Shechem and east of Bethel (Genesis 12:8).

The Lord appeared to Abram at Shechem (Genesis 12:6) to confirm that this land was the Promised Land. Israel was to occupy this land, but sharing in God’s promises required their faith (cp. Numbers 14:1-45; Joshua 1:6-9). • to your descendants: Abram did not yet possess the land; he lived as a temporary settler.

he worshiped the Lord (literally he made proclamation of the Lord by name): Proclaiming the name (identity and character) of the Lord is central to worship and witness (cp. Genesis 4:26; see Exodus 34:5-7). Abram had to distinguish his sacrificial worship from that of the pagan Canaanites.
Abram had to keep moving camp because the Canaanites had the fertile land.
The Nile River provided ample irrigation, so Egypt was often the last region to suffer from famine.

Abram’s scheme was rooted in fear that jeopardized his family and God’s promises. Abram was not walking by faith when he went to Egypt. He stopped building altars and his deceptiveness took center stage. Deception would plague his family throughout Genesis (Genesis 26:1-11; Genesis 27:1-29; Genesis 29:15-30; Genesis 30:34-36; Genesis 31:6-11; Genesis 37:18-35; Genesis 39:7-20). • Abram’s plan was probably based on a social custom whereby a brother arranged the marriage of his sister (cp. Genesis 24:29-61). Abram may have thought that any potential suitor would have to deal with him, giving him time to leave with Sarai. He did not count on Pharaoh’s acting without negotiation (Genesis 12:14-16).

This episode shows that God would not allow Abram to jeopardize his promises. Just after Abram’s obedience to the call, a famine tested his weak faith. God delivered him and his family, even though Abram foolishly used deception rather than trusting in God to preserve him in Egypt. • This story deliberately parallels Israel’s later bondage in Egypt.
