Because of a famine (Genesis 12:10 // Genesis 47:13), Abram/Israel went to Egypt (Genesis 12:10 // Genesis 47:27); there was an attempt to kill the males and save the females (Genesis 12:12 // Exodus 1:22); God plagued Egypt (Genesis 12:17 // Exodus 7:14–11:10); Abram/Israel plundered Egypt (Genesis 12:16 // Exodus 12:35-36); they were expelled (Hebrew shalakh, “send”; Genesis 12:19-20 // Exodus 12:31-33) and ascended to the Negev (Genesis 13:1 // Numbers 13:17, Numbers 13:22). Israel was to believe that God would deliver them from bondage in Egypt through the plagues because their ancestor had already been rescued from bondage in Egypt.

tell them you are my sister: This request occurs three times in Genesis (see also Genesis 20:2; Genesis 26:7). The text explains that this was Abram’s usual strategy (Genesis 20:13), and his son did likewise. This first occasion was outside the land, the second (ch Genesis 20:1-18) within, showing that God protected his promise in both regions.

Sarai was 65 years old, but she lived to be 127; she was like a modern childless woman of about 35. She and Abram came from a noble family (see study note on 11:29), so she was regal in her person and dress. Pharaoh was attracted by her physical appearance and her political assets.

Abram was bound by the king’s gift to an unwanted agreement about Sarai that he could not prevent. His scheme had resulted in a terrible bind that endangered him, Sarai, and the promise. • Abram appeared to prosper from his deception, but the new possessions also caused crises. Abram and Lot had to separate (ch Genesis 13:1-18), and Hagar, an Egyptian maiden, became the mother of the Ishmaelites, perennial enemies of Israel (ch Genesis 16:1-16).
Pharaoh was a title, not a personal name (Genesis 37:36; Exodus 1:15).
God’s intervention rescued Sarai and preserved the marriage to fulfill the covenant promise. Sarai’s restoration to Abram came with a rebuke from Pharaoh on God’s behalf (Genesis 12:18-19).

No answer to Pharaoh’s questions (Genesis 12:18-19) was needed, because the rebuke was followed by expulsion. Pharaoh’s command paralleled God’s command to Abram (Genesis 12:1), but Pharaoh’s demand brought shame and disgrace. God was faithful in preserving his promise.

This story is set in conflict amid God’s blessings. In the opening verses, Abram returns to a place where he had built an altar. Previous events are emphasized as Abram’s return to the land is described (Genesis 13:3-4); Abram renewed his worship and again proclaimed the Lord’s name (cp. Genesis 12:8).
Abram already had powerful resources (Genesis 12:5); his Egyptian sojourn augmented his wealth and power (Genesis 12:16).

Lot was also wealthy, with flocks and herds. Tents figure prominently in Lot’s story (Genesis 13:12). • The Canaanites and Perizzites (see Genesis 34:30; Deuteronomy 7:1; Judges 1:4; Judges 3:5) held the well-watered land; the quarrel between Abram’s and Lot’s herdsmen left Abram more vulnerable to attack.

Abram was concerned that there be no conflict (Hebrew meribah) between them, as they were close relatives (literally brothers). Moses later reproved Israel over the incident in the wilderness at Meribah (Exodus 17:1-7; Numbers 20:1-13) and instructed them on exercising faith in such situations. Meribah thereafter became a watchword for testing and striving with the Lord in unbelief (see Psalm 95:1-11).

Abram, to whom the land was promised, might have told Lot to find his own place. Abram’s generosity was an act of faith; he knew that even if he gave the whole land away, God would still give it to him and his descendants. Abram did not have to cling to things, whereas Lot’s choices were self-seeking.

What appealed to Lot would be short-lived. In the garden of the Lord, Adam and Eve succumbed to their craving for what they saw; Israel was later enslaved in Egypt. Sodom and Gomorrah are reminders of putting intense desires ahead of obedience to God (Genesis 3:5-6; see 1 Jn 2:16). • Zoar was a small town in the plain to which Lot and his daughters later fled (Genesis 19:18-22); it was previously called Bela (Genesis 14:2).

Lot’s choice was totally selfish, without concern for Abram or faith in the Lord. • The region called the whole Jordan Valley (literally the circle of the Jordan) is believed to have been near the south end of the Dead Sea, based on descriptions in ancient records that locate cities of the Plain. This area is now very desolate.
The narrator makes numerous contrasts between Lot and Abram.
The implication is that Lot would not resist Sodom’s influence because he, too, was living for himself.
Abram could give Lot the choice land because he believed in God’s promise. Abram waited for God to give him the land; Lot just took what he wanted.

Hebron was an Anakite city (Numbers 13:22) originally called Kiriath-arba (“city of Arba”), located in forested highlands just north of the Negev (Genesis 12:9; Joshua 17:15). Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all settled there (Genesis 18:1; Genesis 35:27; Genesis 37:14), and Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were buried there (Genesis 23:19; Genesis 35:27-29; Genesis 49:29-32; Genesis 50:13). • Mamre was an Amorite (Genesis 14:13; Genesis 15:16).
Tidal apparently ruled a number of city-states (Goiim, literally nations).

Archaeology has not identified these kings, but similar names from antiquity corroborate the report’s accuracy. The Mesopotamian kings were confederates under a suzerain, apparently Amraphel, who is mentioned first.
In this skirmish typical of ancient politics, powerful kings formed a coalition to subjugate smaller vassal states.

King Kedorlaomer apparently defeated the Siddim Valley kings at an earlier time and put them under tribute for asphalt, olive oil, and copper. In the thirteenth year they refused to send it; in the fourteenth year (Genesis 14:5), the invaders returned to subjugate them again.

This was Kedorlaomer’sChedorlaomer’s war. Under the feudal system of tribal affiliations, those in covenant with him had to fight. It was also Abram’s battle to rescue Lot, and those under treaty with him had to accompany him.
The invaders came down the King’s Highway on the east side of the Jordan Valley to the Gulf of Aqaba, then circled back to the valley of the Dead Sea.

The five cities of the plain were close together at the south end of the Dead Sea. The Mesopotamian kings defeated the frail uprising, looted the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, and carried off Lot with the other captives.

The word Hebrew first occurs here in the Bible. It is not equivalent to the later term Habiru from Egyptian texts; the Habiru were mercenaries that roamed the land in the era of the judges. • Mamre: See study note on 13:18. • relatives: Or allies; literally brothers.

Abram . . . mobilized the 318 trained men who had been born into his household: Abram was a formidable force, an outworking of God’s promise to make him great (Genesis 12:2-3). • Dan was a city about 150 miles north of Abram’s home in Hebron, then named Laish or Leshem (see Joshua 19:47 and study note; Judges 18:29). Dan, whose descendants migrated north in the days of the judges (Judges 18:1-29), had not yet been born (Genesis 30:6). An editor apparently updated the text so that later readers could identify this city.

God could give his people victory over any forces invading the Promised Land. Faithfulness to God was the prerequisite for victory. God promises to bless his people and give them victory over the world. He uses those who respond to his call and can skillfully use weapons of war (cp. Ephesians 4:8; Ephesians 6:10-19).
Damascus was 40 miles north of Dan. Hobah was about 60 miles north of Damascus.
The valley of Shaveh or King’s Valley was probably the Kidron Valley (see 2 Sam 18:18).

Melchizedek means “king of righteousness,” suggesting that he was a righteous servant of God. He was probably a Jebusite priest and king; later authors regarded him as a type of Christ (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:1-19). • Salem is the ancient name of Jerusalem (cp. Psalm 76:2).
By paying a tithe (a tenth) to Melchizedek, Abram acknowledged Melchizedek as a spiritual superior (see Hebrews 7:4) and affirmed that God had given him victory.

Abram knew that accepting the offer of the king of Sodom (see study note on 14:1-2) could make him his ally or subject, as Lot had been. This would jeopardize the fulfillment of God’s promises. Faith looks beyond the riches of the world to the greater blessings that God has in store.
In the words of this oath, Abram may have been clarifying that his God, the Lord (Yahweh), was the God Most High that Melchizedek invoked. Perhaps Melchizedek had never heard the name Yahweh.

Do not be afraid: Abram lacked a son to be his heir. The Lord addressed Abram’s anxiety about the future with comforting words. • I will protect you (literally I will be your shield): The Hebrew word for “shield” (magen) is from the same root as Melchizedek’s word defeated (Genesis 14:20). The Lord who had defeated Abram’s enemies would continue to protect him. • your reward will be great: The promise of offspring (Genesis 12:2-3; cp. Psalm 127:3) was still unfulfilled.

The Lord made a formal covenant with Abram, solemnly confirming the promises made at his call (Genesis 12:1-3). There would be a long period of slavery for Abram’s descendants before these promises would be completely fulfilled.

Using a wordplay, Abram expressed his concern that Eliezer of Damascus (Hebrew dammeseq), a man in Abram’s household, would be his heir (Hebrew ben-mesheq, “son of possession”), as was customary when there was no son.

God affirmed that the promise was for Abram’s own offspring and showed him the stars as a promise of the vast number of descendants that he would have (Genesis 22:17; Genesis 26:4). Paul quotes this promise in Romans 4:18 to underscore the strength of Abram’s faith.

And Abram believed: God made his covenant with a believer; the statement does not indicate when Abram came to faith. The Hebrew text does not link Abram’s belief with the promise of the stars; it just says parenthetically that Abram believed God. Abram already had faith; his departure from Ur was his first great act that demonstrated it (see Hebrews 11:8-10). • God counted him as righteous because of his faith: This central statement about Abram’s saving faith is quoted three times in the New Testament (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6; James 2:23) to support the doctrine of righteousness before God by faith (see also Romans 4:22-23).
With a solemn ceremony, God made a binding covenant with Abram that guaranteed the fulfillment of God’s promises to him.

Obeying God’s instructions, Abram gathered three herd animals for the ceremony and cut them in half. Cutting the animals symbolized the oath, indicating that the covenant maker staked his own life on his word (Jeremiah 34:18).
Vultures are unclean birds of prey that symbolize those who unjustly attack Abraham’s heirs (Genesis 15:13-14).

oppressed: The same word is used in Exodus 1:11-12. Egypt, like predatory birds (Genesis 15:11), would try to destroy Israel and hinder the covenant’s fulfillment. • Apparently 400 years is a round number (also Acts 7:6; cp. Exodus 12:40; Galatians 3:17). Using the chronology in the Hebrew text, the family moved to Egypt around 1876 BC, and the Exodus occurred around 1446 BC (though many scholars date the Exodus later, around 1270 BC; see Exodus Book Introduction, “The Date of the Exodus”).
Not even 400 years of bondage could interfere with God’s plan to fulfill the covenant.

The reasons for Israel’s bondage included God’s justice. God would tolerate the sins of the Amorites until they fully deserved judgment. • do not yet warrant their destruction (literally are not yet full): To give the Promised Land to Israel, the Lord would dispossess the land’s inhabitants in a way that satisfied his justice. The fulfillment of promises to Israel also brought retributive judgment on people of the land (though individuals were saved by faith; see Joshua 2:1-15; Joshua 6:23-25; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). Until then, God would send the family to Egypt where Israel could become a great nation. Seeing all this in advance was terrifying (Genesis 15:12), but it was comforting to know that nothing could interfere with God’s plan.

smoking firepot . . . flaming torch: Fire represented the Lord’s cleansing, consuming zeal and unapproachable holiness (cp. Isaiah 6:3-7). The holy God made (literally cut) a unilateral covenant with Abram; its promises were absolutely sure because they did not depend on what Abram or his descendants might do.

God specified the boundaries of the Promised Land. His clear message to Abram was that despite prospects of death and suffering (enslavement), he and his descendants would eventually receive the promises, for God had sworn an oath (see Hebrews 6:13-14). Nothing can separate God’s people from his love or the fulfillment of his plans (see Romans 8:18-39; 2 Pet 1:3-4).

Abram and Sarai faced the tension of her being barren and beyond childbearing years. By custom, a barren woman could give her servant to her husband as a slave-wife; the child born to that union was considered the wife’s child and could be adopted as the heir. Sarai’s suggestion, unobjectionable by custom, set a problematic human plan in motion. God’s promises would be fulfilled by faith.
While waiting for their promised son to be born, Abram and Sarai attempted an alternate plan that was not in keeping with faith.
Perhaps Hagar expected to become the favored wife instead of Sarai (cp. Proverbs 30:21-23).

The angel of the Lord was the Lord himself (Genesis 16:13; Genesis 21:17; Genesis 22:11-12; Genesis 31:11-13; Genesis 48:16; Exodus 3:2; Exodus 32:34; Judges 6:11, Judges 6:16, Judges 6:22; Judges 13:22-23; Zechariah 3:1-2) but was also distinct from the Lord (Genesis 24:7; 2 Sam 24:16; Zechariah 1:12). The angel of the Lord was probably a theophany (a manifestation of God) or a Christophany (an appearance of the pre-incarnate Messiah; see Genesis 18:1-2; Genesis 19:1; Numbers 22:22; Judges 2:1-4; Judges 5:23; Zechariah 12:8), speaking with the authority of the Lord himself.

The angel’s rhetorical questions encouraged Hagar to pour out her heart to God. When she did, God commanded her to return and submit (Genesis 16:9), promising that her son would have innumerable descendants. The angel of the Lord never referred to Hagar as Abram’s wife, only as Sarai’s servant. She would have Abram’s child, but Ishmael was not central to God’s covenant with Abram.

Hagar’s son would become the father of a great but wild and hostile nation living in the Arabian Desert as perennial enemies of Israel (cp. Genesis 25:18). God blessed Ishmael as Abram’s descendant, but not as the line chosen to carry on the covenant. That blessing was reserved for Abram’s chosen heir.

Names in Genesis often capture the message of a passage and aid the remembrance of the events and their significance in the history of the faith. The name Ishmael, which means “God hears,” commemorates that the Lord . . . heard Hagar’s cry of distress (see also study note on 16:14-15). This name would have greatly comforted Hagar; God listened to her prayers and acknowledged her complaint.
Hagar responded to God’s messages by faith, in her words and in her obedience. • the God who sees me: God knew Hagar’s plight and watched over her.

The names Beer-lahai-roi, which means “well of the Living One who sees me,” and Ishmael (see Genesis 16:11) were a message and a rebuke for Abram and Sarai. God sees affliction and hears the cries of those in need. Sarai and Abram should have prayed rather than taking the fulfillment of the promise into their own hands by following social custom (cp. Genesis 25:21). Giving children to the barren woman is God’s work (Psalm 113:9; cp. 1 Sam 1:1-28; Luke 1:1-25); impossible difficulties cannot be resolved by human intervention. The Lord hears the afflicted, sees them in their need, and will miraculously provide for them.

El-Shaddai: This name for God emphasizes his power (see also Genesis 28:3; Genesis 35:11; Genesis 43:14; Genesis 48:3; Genesis 49:25). • Serve me faithfully and live a blameless life: Being a blessing to the nations required obedience from Abram; his conduct would be guided by Almighty God.

God now gave the family signs that the promises would be fulfilled. He changed Abram’s name to Abraham (Genesis 17:1-8), instituted the rite of circumcision as the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:9-14, Genesis 17:23-27), and changed Sarai’s name to Sarah (Genesis 17:15-22).

God guaranteed his promise by changing Abram’s name. Abram referred to his noble lineage, as Terah was the “exalted father” (Genesis 11:27). His new name, Abraham (Hebrew ’ab hamon) was a wordplay on the promise of his own progeny (see also John 8:31-59; Romans 4:16-17; Galatians 3:7, Galatians 3:15-19, Galatians 3:29). Whenever the new name was used, he and his household would remember that a multitude of nations would issue from him.
kings will be among them! This is the first indication that Israel would become a monarchy (see also Genesis 35:11; Genesis 36:31; Numbers 24:7; Deuteronomy 17:14-18; Deuteronomy 28:36).
The land of Canaan was to be an everlasting possession for the descendants of Abraham; the Lord would be their God forever (see Jeremiah 31:31-40; Zechariah 8:8; Luke 1:68-79; Revelation 21:1-4).
God gave circumcision as a confirming sign that reminded all households of loyalty to the covenant.

will be cut off: This punishment seems to have several applications. A person could be exiled from society or put to death by the community; most often it warned that a person might die prematurely as God cut him off from the land of the living (see Exodus 31:14; Leviticus 7:20-27; Leviticus 17:3-4; Leviticus 20:17-18; Leviticus 23:28-29; Numbers 15:30-31; see also Psalm 31:22; Ezekiel 21:4; Romans 9:3; Romans 11:22). Failure to be circumcised was a serious violation (see Exodus 4:24-26; cp. Galatians 5:2-4).
Sarah: The new name, fitting for one who would be the mother of kings, was a milestone in Sarah’s calling and brought attention to the promise.
Abraham laughed (Hebrew yitskhaq) because the promise seemed unbelievable; he had begun to believe that his line would come through Ishmael. But Abraham and Sarah would have a son of their own.

The name Isaac (Hebrew yitskhaq, “he laughs”) would constantly recall Abraham’s disbelieving laughter when he heard the promise. It was also a reminder of God’s favor and his pleasure in the birth (cp. Genesis 21:6).
Ishmael would not be abandoned; his family would prosper (see Genesis 25:13-16), but the covenant promises were for Isaac.

Having received God’s word about Isaac, Abraham immediately complied with God’s instructions. He implemented the rite of circumcision as an act of faith; it signified their participation in the covenant (cp. Romans 4:11-12; Galatians 5:2-6, Galatians 5:11; Galatians 6:15; Philippians 3:2-3; Colossians 2:11-12; 1 Pet 3:21).

The Lord’s visit to Abraham set the time for Isaac’s birth. The three visitors were probably the Lord and two angels (see study note on 16:7). Abraham’s peaceful and generous reception of the visitors contrasts sharply with the chaos and corruption of Sodom (ch Genesis 19:1-38). Eating together was important in making or confirming covenants; when God was ready to fulfill the covenant promise, he came in person to share a meal with Abraham. Fellowship with God has always been signified by a communal meal (see Exodus 24:9-11; Matthew 26:17-30 // Luke 22:7-38; Acts 2:42; 1 Cor 11:20-34).
Abraham received his visitors as very important guests, perhaps realizing that they were messengers from God.

My lord: The Hebrew text uses ’adonay (“Lord”), the word that is usually reserved for God. In Hebrew tradition, it was spoken in places where the holy name Yahweh (the Lord) was in the text. Perhaps the text uses ’adonay rather than the more common ’adoni to show that this was the angel of the Lord—i.e., the Lord himself (see study note on 16:7). We don’t know whether Abraham knew his visitors’ identity at the outset, but by the story’s end Abraham certainly knew he had been talking with God.
The visitors’ rhetorical question focuses attention on Sarah, whom the visitors knew by name.
I will return: The Hebrew verb means “to intervene in someone’s life to change their destiny.” The statement announced a coming dramatic change.

Sarah thought her disbelieving laughter was hidden, but God knows human hearts (see Psalm 69:5; Proverbs 20:27; Mark 4:22; Luke 8:43-48; Hebrews 4:13), whether they stagger at the promises or step out in faith (see Hebrews 11:11-12).

Is anything too hard for the Lord? The question is rhetorical. God is able to do marvelous things. Nothing is incredible to those in covenant fellowship with the Lord, because nothing is too difficult for him.

God took Abraham into his confidence as his prophet (Genesis 18:16-21; see Genesis 20:7); Abraham, in turn, interceded for Sodom (Genesis 18:23-32; see Hebrews 7:23-26). God is able to do whatever he chooses to do; this passage affirms that it will be just and right.

Abraham was responsible for teaching his descendants righteousness and justice so that they might enjoy God’s blessings. It was important for Abraham to know how God’s righteousness was at work in judgment.
a great outcry: See Ezekiel 16:49-50.

The omniscient God was cautious in his judgment: He knew the sins of Sodom and Gomorrah, but this close scrutiny communicated God’s justice in human terms—he would not destroy the people of the plain unless he was absolutely sure they were wicked.

Abraham probably thought there were more righteous people in Sodom and Gomorrah than there were (see study note on 19:14). In his concern for them, he approached the Lord with a legal appeal based on God’s justice. His prayer seems too bold at times, as though he were bargaining with God, but he approached God with genuine humility and reverence. He did not try to talk God into doing something against his will, but prayed for the well-being of others (contrast Lot’s prayer, Genesis 19:18-23). God is a righteous judge; righteousness exalts a nation (Proverbs 14:34), and righteous people help to preserve society (cp. Matthew 5:13).

The two angels also first appeared to Abraham as men (Genesis 18:2). • Lot was no longer living in tents next to Sodom (Genesis 13:12)—he had become a citizen and leader in Sodom, sitting there at the entrance of the city. Community leaders (elders) usually congregated in the gates, where legal and business transactions were publicly finalized (cp. Genesis 23:18; Job 29:7, Job 29:12-17). As a righteous man (2 Pet 2:7-8), Lot tried to modify the townspeople’s wickedness by giving advice on good living (cp. Genesis 19:9). Although he denounced gross evil, Lot preferred Sodom’s sumptuous lifestyle to life in the hills (cp. Genesis 13:10-11), where there was clean living but no “good life.” As long as the Lord left Lot and his family alone in Sodom, he lived comfortably there and kept his personal belief in God; but finally, he could not hold to both. Sodom would have destroyed Lot if the Lord had not destroyed Sodom. • This account showed Israel that God is the righteous judge of the whole earth (Genesis 18:25) who will judge evildoers with justice and equity. In wicked societies, moral and ethical failures lead to social injustice.

The two angels who were with the Lord at Mamre (cp. Genesis 18:2, Genesis 18:22) visited Sodom reluctantly, knowing what kind of people lived there. Despite Lot’s hospitality, they preferred lodging in the square to entering Lot’s house.

The Canaanites were an evil, corrupting people. God judged their morally bankrupt civilization and warned others against becoming like them. It was difficult to get Lot and his family out of Sodom; it was more difficult to get Sodom out of Lot and his family. This chapter helped later Israelites to understand the moral and spiritual threat of the peoples living in and around the Promised Land, such as the Canaanites and Lot’s descendants, the Moabites and the Ammonites (see Numbers 22:1–25:18; Deuteronomy 23:3-6; Joshua 24:9; Judges 10:7-9; Judges 11:4-5; 1 Sam 10:27; 1 Kgs 11:1-3; 2 Kgs 24:2).
The townsmen’s vileness was matched by Lot’s hypocrisy (Genesis 19:6-9).

Lot opposed homosexuality and rape and rebuked their wicked plans, but he was hypocritically willing to sacrifice his daughters to fend off the townsmen’s vice. Lot had originally pitched his tent next to Sodom; now Sodom controlled his life.
The men of the city were enraged by Lot’s attempts to curtail their wickedness. Lot had apparently not condemned them before, since they were amazed that he now judged them.
Lot’s warning words were not taken seriously because of his hypocrisy. It seemed that there would not be even ten righteous people in the city.

Lot escaped judgment by God’s grace, but his heart was still in Sodom. Israel would forever remember Lot as lingering, halting, and being dragged to safety by angels. The Lord mercifully spared Lot for Abraham’s sake (Genesis 18:23; Genesis 19:29). Lot deserved judgment for his way of life, but he was a believer at heart and the Lord rescued him (2 Pet 2:7-8). • Lot is not alone in his conflicted lifestyle. Countless believers fall in with a corrupt world rather than flee a doomed society. God’s people, living in a pagan world, must remain separate (1 Jn 2:15-17). The corrupt world system awaits God’s coming judgment, which will be far greater than the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Matthew 11:23-24).
Lot demanded a concession from the angels even after he was delivered. He wanted to live in the small town of Zoar (little place).
Cp. Luke 17:29. The eruption of Vesuvius and the destruction of Pompeii in AD 79, as well as recent natural disasters, show how quickly a thorough catastrophe like this could happen.

looked back: The verb indicates prolonged, intense gazing toward the world she loved, not a curious glance (Genesis 15:5; Exodus 33:8; Numbers 21:9; 1 Sam 2:32; cp. Exodus 3:6). Lot’s wife was too attached to Sodom to follow God’s call of grace, so she was included in the judgment as she lingered on the valley slopes. Christ’s return to judge the world will be as sudden and devastating as the destruction of Sodom (Luke 17:32-37). Those who crave the life of this wicked world will lose this world and the next.

God honored Abraham’s intercession (cp. Genesis 18:23-32), but Lot’s entire world was gone because he lived by instinct and desire, not by faith in God. He could no longer live in the good land he selfishly chose for himself (Genesis 13:10-13; cp. Matthew 16:26; 2 Cor 5:7).

The character of Lot’s daughters was formed by Sodom’s culture more than by their father’s heritage, so they had no qualms about having children by their drunk father (cp. Genesis 9:21-22). They saw no other way to carry on their line.

The poverty of the cave contrasts with the wealth Lot shared with Abram and the good life he lived in Sodom. Abraham would father a righteous nation (Genesis 17:1), but Lot and his daughters gave birth to a new Sodom.

The daughters’ plan worked, and they each became pregnant by their own father. From these two incest-born sons came two perennial enemies of Israel, the nations of Moab and Ammon. Their grotesque wickedness was due in part to their origin. • Both daughters chose ambiguous names that hinted at their actions without raising the suspicions of those who did not know the stories.
Gerar was near the coast in Philistine land, about twelve miles south of Gaza and fifty miles southwest of Hebron.

This second “sister story” in Genesis (cp. Genesis 12:10-20) occurred shortly before Sarah became pregnant with Isaac (ch Genesis 21:1-34). On both occasions, God protected Abraham and Sarah’s marriage in purity for the sake of the covenant promises. Participation in God’s plan requires separation from worldly corruption. • This story took place in the Promised Land; it showed Israel how God intervened in people’s lives to fulfill his plan, how God continued to protect them against threats from other tribes, and how God used his chosen people to mediate his relationship with the nations. • God’s preventing the destruction of Abraham’s marriage by adultery reminded the Israelites to keep their marriages morally and racially pure (Ezra 9:1-4; Nehemiah 13:23-27; Malachi 2:10-17); they should not allow any opportunity for temptation (Exodus 20:14, Exodus 20:17; Leviticus 20:10; Leviticus 21:13-15). Adultery would eventually destroy the covenant and the covenant people.

Abraham told the same lie to Abimelech that he had told to Pharaoh (Genesis 12:13); Isaac would later do the same (Genesis 26:1-11), probably having learned this tactic from his father. • Abimelech (literally my father the king) was probably a title like “Pharaoh” (Genesis 37:36; Exodus 1:15), not a proper name (see study note on Gen 26:1).
that night God came . . . in a dream: God urgently intervened to stop Abimelech from violating Sarah’s purity shortly before God’s promise was fulfilled (Genesis 18:10; Genesis 21:1-3).
God gave Abimelech a stern warning against committing adultery; it was a capital offense (cp. Exodus 20:14), viewed throughout the ancient Near East as a “great sin” (Genesis 20:9).

Abimelech was innocent (Genesis 20:6); his conscience was clear. Nonetheless, he was about to commit adultery, and ignorance does not excuse guilt (Leviticus 4:13-14). • will you destroy an innocent nation? Abimelech’s appeal to God echoes Abraham’s earlier words (cp. Genesis 18:23-32) and rebukes Abraham’s lack of faith on this occasion.

Because Abimelech acted with a clear conscience, God kept him from sinning. God will graciously help those who try to do what is right. When people act with reverence toward God, God gives them more revelation and draws them into more specific faith (see Acts 10:1-48).

Abraham’s prayer saved the king’s life and restored his family (Genesis 20:17-18). Abimelech learned that Abraham’s God was sovereign, and that Abraham, God’s prophet, had received God’s revelation and would intercede for others (see Numbers 12:13; Deuteronomy 9:20), even if he did not always live up to the office.

Abraham had earned rebukes from Abimelech and from God (cp. Genesis 12:17-19). Abimelech was angry that Abraham’s deception had made him guilty of this great sin (see study note on 20:3-7). He knew that taking a married woman into his harem was wrong.

Abraham’s duplicity was not a momentary loss of faith. Despite the rebuke he received in Egypt, he practiced this strategy wherever he went (cp. Genesis 12:12-13). Living by faith requires perseverance.

Abimelech secured his reputation as a good man (see study note on 20:4-5) and demonstrated his integrity. He made amends by allowing Abraham to live in the region and by giving him slaves, livestock (cp. Genesis 21:27), and 1,000 pieces of silver to compensate . . . for any wrong done to Sarah.

The infertility suggests that some time had passed. God controls births; he opens and closes wombs (Genesis 25:21; Genesis 29:31; Genesis 30:2, Genesis 30:17, Genesis 30:22-23; 1 Sam 1:19-20; Psalm 113:9; Psalm 127:3; Luke 1:13).
See Genesis 18:10.
Abraham responded in faith by naming his son Isaac and circumcising him according to the terms of the covenant (see Genesis 17:9-14).
Isaac was born twenty-five years after the promise was first given (cp. Genesis 12:4).

Sarah’s wordplay on the name Isaac (Hebrew yitskhaq, “he laughs”) shows that the laughter of unbelief when the promise was given (Genesis 18:12) had changed to the laughter of joy at its fulfillment. Isaac’s name could refer to the pleasure of God and of his parents at his birth. Sarah knew that everyone who heard about this would laugh with her and rejoice at the news.
Sarah was filled with joy and praise for this amazing event—only God could enable her to have a child.

The feast for Isaac’s weaning probably occurred when he was three and Ishmael was about seventeen years old (Genesis 16:16). Sarah saw Ishmael making fun of her son, Isaac: The verb metsakheq (“making fun of”) is related to the word for “laughter”; this theme (Genesis 21:6) is given a sour twist by Ishmael’s mockery.

God used the incident of Ishmael’s mocking Isaac to separate Ishmael and Hagar from the family and the child of promise. They would constantly threaten the promised descendant if they remained with the family.
Earlier, Sarah mistreated Hagar and pressured her to flee (Genesis 16:6); when Hagar’s son mistreated Isaac, Sarah demanded that that slave woman and her son leave.
Abraham was upset by Sarah’s demand to oust Hagar and Ishmael. God told him to comply, assuring Abraham that Ishmael would also have a future as Abraham’s offspring.

God again rescued Hagar in the wilderness and guaranteed her future (cp. Genesis 16:7-14). This passage is similar to ch Genesis 16:1-16, but the differences are great. Here, Hagar and Ishmael are rescued, but there is no commemorative naming. God’s earlier promise to Hagar is reiterated, but this time Hagar is not told to return to Sarah. The repeated motifs on the two occasions confirm God’s sovereign plan for Hagar and Ishmael. As Joseph later told Pharaoh, a twofold event demonstrated God’s confirmation (Genesis 41:32). God did not abandon Hagar and Ishmael but met them in their despair (cp. Genesis 16:7), provided sustenance for them, and promised again that Ishmael would found a great nation (Genesis 21:13; cp. Genesis 16:11-12). Paul uses this event in his letter to the Galatians to illustrate how God’s people must relinquish all that threatens the fulfillment of God’s promise (Galatians 4:21-31).
a hundred yards (literally a bowshot): This description connects with Ishmael’s vocation (Genesis 21:20).

Abimelech pressed for the treaty so that Abraham would not cheat or deceive him. Abimelech knew that God was blessing Abraham even though Abraham was not entirely trustworthy (Genesis 20:9-10). This sad contradiction made the treaty necessary. By contrast, God’s faithful people are exhorted to speak the truth (Ephesians 4:15, Ephesians 4:25), and Jesus warned against manipulating truth by the clever use of oaths (Matthew 5:37; James 5:12).

This passage, at its climax, explains the name of Beersheba, Abraham’s home (Genesis 21:31-34). Beersheba reflected the covenant Abraham made with the residents of the land, which enabled him to dwell there in peace and prosperity. God’s promise was coming to fruition (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 13:14-17; Genesis 15:7, Genesis 15:18-21; Genesis 17:8).

The motif of the well appears again (cp. Genesis 16:14; Genesis 21:19). God provided water (a symbol of blessing) in the barren wilderness and later even brought water out of a rock for Israel (Exodus 15:22-27; Exodus 17:1-7; Numbers 20:1-13).

Abraham’s gifts to Abimelech (cp. Genesis 20:14) secured his legal right to dwell peaceably in the land and to claim ownership of the well. Beersheba marked one more step toward the fulfillment of God’s promise.

The Philistines in Genesis are different from the Philistines of Judges through Kings. The earlier Philistines had Semitic names (e.g., Abimelech) and Canaanite culture. The later Philistines were apparently of Greek origin, with Greek customs and culture. They seem to have arrived in Canaan by sea from the Aegean area around 1200 BC, during the time of the judges. Probably the name of the later Philistines was used here simply to describe the region’s earlier inhabitants.

A tamarisk tree requires a lot of water; this act indicated Abraham’s security in his land rights and his faith that God would provide water in this desert area. He settled as a foreigner in the land, but dwelling under his tree was a sign of peaceful security (cp. Zechariah 3:10). • there he worshiped the Lord: See study note on 12:8.

Some time later: Abraham had sent Ishmael away and settled in the land. Now God tested Abraham’s faith by telling him to give up Isaac. This pushed the limits of logic and of Abraham’s knowledge of God. Would he still obey when God seemed to be working against him and against the covenant? Would he cling to the boy or surrender him to God (see Exodus 13:11-13)? Did he believe that God would still keep his word and bless the world through Abraham’s offspring?
The greatest test in Abraham’s life came after he had received the promised child following a long wait. He had grown to love Isaac and had enjoyed his presence for a number of years.

Obedience to God’s earlier call (Genesis 12:1-3) was rewarded with great blessing; now Abraham had the opportunity to show even greater obedience. • Take your son . . . Isaac, whom you love so much: By this detailed description of Isaac, God reminded Abraham that the young man was his beloved son, and intensified his awareness of the cost of the sacrifice. • The name Moriah is explained by the Chronicler (2 Chr 3:1) as the place of the later Temple Mount in Jerusalem. • Go: By wording the command in this way, God helped Abraham to obey by recalling his former call (cp. Genesis 12:1-3).
Abraham’s immediate, unquestioning obedience is almost as astounding as the test.

We will worship there, and then we will come (or We will worship there so that we may come back): Abraham’s amazing statement makes us wonder what he was thinking. Abraham knew that God had planned the future of the covenant around Isaac and that God wanted him to sacrifice Isaac. He could not reconcile these things in his mind; he could only do what God commanded him to do, and leave the future to God (cp. Hebrews 11:17-19).
In response to Isaac’s question, Abraham again showed his faith in the Lord, saying God will provide, although he was not sure how. This theme is central to the entire narrative.

God’s intervention was dramatic and instructive, confirming that he never intended for Isaac to be sacrificed. God later made it clear that child sacrifice was an abomination to him (see Leviticus 18:21; Leviticus 20:1-5; Deuteronomy 18:10; 2 Kgs 16:2-3; Isaiah 57:5; Jeremiah 32:35). God wanted Abraham to sacrifice his own will and surrender it to God, and when he did, God intervened. This passage sets a pattern for all sacrificial worshipers. Like Abraham, true worshipers of God know that everything belongs to God—it all came from God and must therefore be acknowledged as God’s possession. A true worshiper holds nothing back but obediently gives God what he asks, trusting that God will provide for all needs, and then discovering through experience that God always does so.
The angel of the Lord stopped Abraham just as he was ready to plunge the knife into his son.

Now God knew that Abraham would hold nothing back from him, that he did truly fear God. To fear the Lord means to reverence him as sovereign, trust him implicitly, and obey him without protest. The sacrifice that pleases God is a heart broken of self-will, surrendered to God (Psalm 40:6-8; Psalm 51:17) and offering its best to God. • You have not withheld: Cp. Romans 8:32, which uses the same verb (“spare”) as the Greek Old Testament uses here. If God gave us his dearest possession, he will surely provide all things for us.

God provided a ram caught by its horns in a thicket for the sacrifice. God graciously allowed Abraham to substitute an animal sacrifice in place of Isaac. Later, all Israel would offer animals to the Lord, knowing that God’s grace had provided this substitution (Exodus 29:10; Leviticus 4:15; Leviticus 16:20-22). In the New Testament, God substituted his only son for all humanity; the perfect sacrifice was made once and for all (Isaiah 53:6, Isaiah 53:10; John 1:29; Hebrews 7:27; Hebrews 10:1-14; 1 Pet 3:18).

As with many patriarchal narratives, the heart of the matter is retained through commemorative naming. Yahweh-Yireh . . . means “the Lord will provide” (see Genesis 22:8). That Abraham used the holy name in this act shows that the patriarchs knew the name Yahweh (cp. Exodus 6:2-3) but not its full meaning (see study note on Exod 6:2-3). • To this day: Later Israelites understood this passage as a lesson about their own worship in Jerusalem. Abraham’s sacrifice took place on the mountain of the Lord, later the location of the Temple in Jerusalem (see study note on 22:2). Three times a year, the people of Israel brought their best to God as a sacrifice, trusting that he would continue to provide for their needs.

After the event, God again confirmed his covenant with Abraham (cp. Genesis 15:5, Genesis 15:18-21; Genesis 17:3-8). His descendants would be numerous like the stars in the sky (cp. Genesis 26:4), like the sand on the seashore (cp. Genesis 32:12), and like the dust of the earth (cp. Genesis 13:16; Genesis 28:14).
by my own name: There is no higher name by which God can swear (Hebrews 6:13-17).

Joshua and Old Testament Israel partially fulfilled the promise that Abraham’s descendants would conquer the cities (literally take possession of the gates) of God’s enemies; this will be fulfilled fully by the church (cp. Matthew 16:18 and study note there).

Abraham passed the test of faith; from this point, his task was to pass the covenant blessings to Isaac. He purchased a burial plot (ch Genesis 23:1-20), acquired a wife for Isaac (ch Genesis 24:1-67), and distributed his property (Genesis 25:1-11).
Milcah, Nahor’s wife, was also his niece (see Genesis 11:29).
A report came from the east that Abraham’s brother Nahor (see Genesis 11:27-29) was flourishing. The actors in the following narrative are introduced here.
Uz might have been Job’s forefather (Job 1:1).

Bethuel was the youngest of Nahor’s eight sons by Milcah; he was the father of Rebekah, Isaac’s future wife (see Genesis 24:15, Genesis 24:67). Rebekah would follow Sarah as matriarch of the clan (Genesis 23:1-2).
Sarah was 127 years old: Isaac was 37 at this time (cp. Genesis 17:17). • Hebron: See study note on 13:18.

When Sarah . . . died, Abraham acquired a parcel of land for a burial place. This transaction was the first sign that a permanent transition had taken place, as people were normally buried in their ancestral homeland (cp. Genesis 49:29–50:13). In burying Sarah, Abraham detached from his just-mentioned ancestral home (where his relatives still lived, Genesis 22:20-24); his future would be in Canaan, where his descendants would realize the promise.

Abraham bargained with local Hittite elders for a piece of land for a burial site. These Hittites had apparently migrated south to Canaan from the great Hittite empire in eastern Asia Minor (modern Turkey; cp. Genesis 10:15). • Abraham was a stranger and a foreigner among these people; his hope was in God’s promise that he would eventually possess the land.

my lord, you are an honored prince: Either Abraham was highly regarded by these people, or they were politely appealing to his generosity. • Choose the finest. . . . No one here will refuse: They were willing to accommodate his request, especially if they could legally obligate him to themselves (Genesis 23:11).
Abraham wanted to buy Ephron’s cave at Machpelah, but Ephron wanted him to buy the entire field.

This would be a permanent burial place for Abraham’s family. The site was near Mamre (Genesis 23:19), where Abraham lived (see Genesis 13:18; Genesis 14:13; Genesis 18:1). Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob and Leah would all be buried in this cave (Genesis 23:19; Genesis 25:9; Genesis 35:27-29; Genesis 49:29-31; Genesis 50:13), their permanent place in the Promised Land.

Ephron did not intend to give the cave to Abraham; Abraham was expected to “give” the full price in return. Ephron wanted to sell as much as he could to avoid responsibility for caring for the cave and to receive as high a price as possible.
Abraham didn’t want the whole field, but he was willing to take it to get the cave.
400 pieces of silver was a very high price. Ephron’s politeness was typical of the bargaining process.

Abraham paid the amount and finalized the transaction, avoiding indebtedness by accepting no gifts from the people (cp. Genesis 14:21-24). The Hittite elders witnessed the transaction, ensuring that no one could challenge Abraham’s full ownership of the land. The transaction took place at the city gate, where public legal and business dealings were conducted (cp. Genesis 19:1). The land became Abraham’s permanent possession, a down payment on God’s promise to give him the land. Abraham knew that God’s promise was not fulfilled (Genesis 12:7) by this acquisition, so he planned for the future. By buying land for his dead, he declared that God’s promises do not end with this life. This is the hope of all who die in faith.

Confident in the Lord’s promise, Abraham had his chief servant (probably Eliezer, Genesis 15:2) swear to find a wife among Abraham’s relatives in his homeland, some 450 miles away. Abraham was faithful to the covenant by preparing for Isaac’s future.

Isaac’s marriage to Rebekah ensured that God’s plan would continue into the next generation. God showed covenant faithfulness by working through his faithful people (Genesis 24:12, Genesis 24:27, Genesis 24:49).
Putting his hand under Abraham’s thigh (cp. Genesis 47:29), the servant took a very solemn oath, assuming the burden of completing this mission.
Isaac knew how wicked and threatening the local Canaanite people were, so he maintained separation from them (cp. Genesis 26:34-35; Genesis 27:46; Genesis 28:8-9).
Under no circumstances was the servant to take Isaac from the Promised Land to seek a wife. Abraham ensured Isaac’s safety and secured God’s promises in the land of blessing.

Aram-naharaim (“Aram of the two rivers”) was also called Paddan-aram (“the field of Aram,” cp. Genesis 25:20). It was a two-week journey in each direction, so the servant had ten . . . camels for provisions and gifts (Genesis 24:22, Genesis 24:53).
The servant obeyed his master’s instructions and trusted God to lead him to the right woman.

The servant faithfully carried out the mission, and he glorified God in displaying faithful covenant love for Abraham’s family by bringing all the details together. God sovereignly worked behind the scenes to accomplish his will through the circumstances of those acting responsibly in faith.

Abraham’s future daughter-in-law manifested hospitality and industry like Abraham’s (see Genesis 18:1-8). Ten thirsty camels could drink 250 gallons of water, so a woman who would work that hard for a stranger was certainly not lazy, but generous and hospitable.
The servant received a precise, immediate answer to his prayer for guidance.
The servant showed his gratitude by giving the girl expensive jewelry.
God led the servant to Abraham’s family.
Rebekah again showed kindness by offering lodging for the servant and food for his camels.
The servant bowed to the ground and worshiped the Lord for his loyal love and faithfulness in guiding him to the exact family he sought.

The Lord has shown unfailing love and faithfulness to my master: These words express this chapter’s message (cp. Genesis 24:48). Believers can trust the Lord’s leading because he is sovereign in all things. He never leaves his people to their own resources in carrying out his covenant work.

Laban . . . ran: He was not going to miss the chance to marry his sister off and receive more gifts. Laban’s response to the servant’s wealth foreshadows his avaricious character (see Genesis 24:54-56 and study note; Genesis 29:21-27; Genesis 30:27-36; Genesis 31:1-13).

The servant was not diverted from his mission; he insisted on telling his story before he would eat. He recounted his mission and acknowledged God’s providence in directing him to Rebekah before attending to his personal needs. The servant wanted everyone to know that this was God’s work, not a chance or humanly arranged meeting.

The way that God directed this event from behind the scenes is different than in most of Genesis, but it is true to how the life of faith normally works. Faith, expressed in personal prayer and obedience, looks for evidence of God’s working. Believers usually have to make wise choices and remain faithful to the covenant, trusting that God will guide them through the circumstances of life to accomplish his will.
Following his testimony about God’s guidance, the servant secured the family’s blessing and permission to take Rebekah to his master’s son Isaac.
The servant gave expensive gifts to Rebekah, her mother, and her brother to conclude the arrangements.

It was hard for Rebekah’s family to let her go so suddenly, and Laban may have hoped to gain more wealth. However, the servant had sworn an oath and would not rest until it was completed. There was no reason for him to stay.

Rebekah’s decision to leave immediately to be with her new husband settled the impasse. Rebekah submitted to the Lord’s obvious leading. Young women were normally eager to marry (not to marry was a catastrophe), and later accounts of Laban suggest why Rebekah preferred to leave (cp. Genesis 31:14-15). Rebekah displayed faithful love to the servant, Abraham’s family, and Isaac by going to be Isaac’s wife.

At Rebekah’s departure, her family invoked the blessing that she would be a mother of many millions and that her descendants would conquer . . . their enemies. Rebekah’s marriage to Isaac was part of God’s plan to bless all humankind (Genesis 12:1-3).
Isaac lived in the Negev, in the southern part of Canaan.
Isaac was 40 years old when he married Rebekah (Genesis 25:20), so Abraham was 140 (Genesis 21:5).
Exactly when Abraham married . . . Keturah is unknown. It was probably, but not necessarily, after Sarah’s death.
Though Abraham had sons by another wife, he safeguarded Isaac’s inheritance and blessing.
The birth of these nations from Abraham partially fulfilled God’s promise to him (Genesis 12:2; Genesis 17:4).
Sheba and Dedan: Cp. Genesis 10:7. Abraham’s descendants probably settled in these regions and became identified by their names, along with people of other lineage.
Abraham loved all his sons, so before he died, he gave them gifts and sent them away as he had sent Ishmael (Genesis 21:8-14). In this way, he preserved Isaac’s position as his heir.

Abraham’s death is recorded before the births of Jacob and Esau, but he lived until they were fifteen years old (Genesis 25:19-26; cp. Genesis 21:5; Genesis 25:26). This literary arrangement closes Abraham’s story before focusing on Isaac’s family.

God’s blessing transferred to Isaac; Abraham’s other sons had been sent away. Isaac lived near Beer-lahai-roi—a special place where God had answered prayer (Genesis 16:14) and where Isaac waited on the Lord (Genesis 24:62).
This record lists Ishmael’s descendants before tracing Isaac’s (Genesis 25:19–35:29), which is in keeping with the literary arrangement of Genesis (see Genesis Book Introduction, “Summary”).
Ishmael’s twelve sons fulfilled God’s promise of blessing (Genesis 17:20).
Havilah was a region in north-central Arabia. • Shur was a region between Beersheba and Egypt. • in open hostility toward all their relatives: The wording is close to that of Genesis 16:12.

Isaac . . . married Rebekah: Isaac’s marriage tied him and his family even more closely to Abraham’s ancestors. Had he married a Canaanite, the covenant faith would have been imperiled by this corrupt, syncretistic people.
Jacob’s struggle for supremacy began before the twins were born (see Hosea 12:3).
This account of the family of Isaac, the chosen son of Abraham, mostly recounts Jacob’s struggle for the blessing (Genesis 25:27-34; chs Genesis 27:1–33:20).

For twenty years, Rebekah was barren (cp. Genesis 25:20, Genesis 25:26), like Sarah (see Genesis 16:1). This condition tested their faith (see study note on 16:1-3). How could they be childless when God promised that nations would issue from them? • Isaac pleaded with the Lord and the Lord answered Isaac’s prayer. Isaac apparently learned from his father’s mistake and responded in faith.
When the pregnancy was difficult, Rebekah went to ask the Lord about it, probably by visiting a prophet—perhaps Abraham (Genesis 20:7; see study note on 25:7-8).

rivals: Jacob and Esau fought in the womb, and their descendants (Israel and Edom) fought continuously throughout their history. In their many conflicts, Israel achieved supremacy over Edom. • your older son will serve your younger son: God’s choice of the younger son over the elder ran against natural order (cp. Genesis 48:12-14; see Malachi 1:1-3; Romans 9:11-16).
When the twins were born, the unusual circumstances inspired each boy’s name and hinted at what would happen to them in the future.

Two wordplays anticipate Esau’s later life. Esau sounds like Hebrew se‘ar, which means “hair”; Esau’s later homeland, Edom, was known as Seir (“hairy”) because it was wooded (as though covered with hair). • red (Hebrew ’admoni) sounds like Esau’s other name, Edom (Genesis 25:27-34); Edom had red soil. • Esau’s >hair was like the fur coat of an animal, foreshadowing his unspiritual character (Genesis 25:34; Hebrews 12:16; cp. Leviticus 26:22; Deuteronomy 7:22; 1 Cor 15:32). The description of the child uses words that highlight the Edomites’ nature.

The name Jacob (Hebrew ya‘aqob, from Hebrew ‘aqeb, “heel, footprint”) was originally positive, meaning “protect” (like a rear guard), but it took on the negative meaning of “heel grabber” or “deceiver” in the context of Jacob’s deceptive, grasping, usurping character (see Genesis 27:36).

Esau was a skillful hunter and an outdoorsman—a wild man who loved wild country. Jacob had a quiet (or even) temperament and preferred to stay at home (literally dwelling in tents)—i.e., he was civilized.

Jacob and Esau each developed in accord with his initial characteristics (Genesis 25:24-26). Esau, the reddish, hairy man, cared about physical things rather than spiritual things (see Hebrews 12:16); he was finally overcome by physical appetites and sold his birthright. Jacob, the heel grabber, knew the birthright’s value and drove a ruthless bargain to gain it presumptuously from his brother.
The parents each practiced favoritism. • because: Isaac’s love for Esau was conditioned upon his son’s performance. Rebekah’s love for Jacob was constant and unconditional.

Ironically, Jacob proved the more cunning hunter. The word cooking (Hebrew wayyazed, “boiling”) sounds like the word for “hunter” (Hebrew tsayid). While boiling stew, Jacob was laying a trap for the hairy red animal. He may have waited a long time for this opportunity. This word for “boil” was also used for presumptuous action (like water boiling over the rim of the pot). Jacob overstepped his boundaries when he seized the promise for himself. By contrast, Abraham knew the promise was his and was secure in giving the land away (see study note on 13:8-13). • Esau was exhausted and hungry, but his life was not in danger (Genesis 25:32; see study note on 25:33-34).

Esau was preoccupied with his appetite. Being driven by one’s appetites leaves no place for spiritual values. The text emphasizes this by using a Hebrew word (translated give) that was normally used for feeding animals. • Edom, which means “red”: See study note on 25:25.

Jacob was the better hunter on this occasion, but great danger lay in exercising such strong ambition. God’s people should desire the things of God, but they must not seek them in the flesh (see Zechariah 4:6; Galatians 5:16-17; Ephesians 6:10-12). The Lord dealt severely with Jacob to purge him of carnal methods. He later received the promise not as crafty Jacob the usurper, but as Israel (meaning, “God fights”), with God fighting on his behalf (Genesis 32:28).

Esau eagerly took Jacob’s bait and fell into the trap. He ate and left too quickly to have been near death (Genesis 25:32). The final comment on the passage explains that Esau showed contempt for his birthright, considering it worthless (Hebrews 12:16). It is foolish to sacrifice spiritual blessings to satisfy physical appetites (cp. Genesis 3:6).

This Abimelech is probably not the man in ch Genesis 20:1-18, for these events could have been 90 years apart. Possibly Abimelech was a dynastic name or title (a later King Achish, 1 Sam 21:10, was also called Abimelech, Psalm 34:1).
In this digression from Jacob’s story, Isaac’s prosperity (ch Genesis 26:1-35) shows that the blessing had passed to him (cp. Genesis 25:11) despite his failures of faith.

The Lord assured Isaac that the covenant promises (cp. Genesis 12:2-3; Genesis 15:5-8; Genesis 17:3-8; Genesis 22:15-18; Genesis 28:13-14) would pass to him because Abraham faithfully listened to God and obeyed all his requirements, commands, decrees, and instructions. These terms were later used in Deuteronomy to describe God’s full legal covenant with Israel. An Israelite reader would immediately think of the complete Torah when hearing these words and be prompted to obey God’s law as Abraham did, though Abraham had only a few commands from the Lord. Through these words, the text emphasizes that Abraham would have obeyed the later commands if he had had them, because he was an obedient servant of the Lord.

While staying in Gerar, Isaac, like his father, deceived people into believing that his wife was his sister. Some suppose that this story duplicates the stories of Abraham’s deception (Genesis 12:10-20; Genesis 20:1-18), but the differences are greater than the similarities, and the son’s repetition of his father’s lie is natural. Through numerous parallels with Abraham, ch Genesis 26:1-35 shows how God’s plan continued with Isaac. Even when Isaac jeopardized the covenant as his father had, God prevented disaster and preserved the marriage. Abraham’s descendants would be blessed because of Abraham, but they had to exercise their own faith to enjoy the blessings. Genuine faith in God’s promises engenders a fearless walk with him; cowering in fear endangers the blessing and mocks the faith.

Abimelech . . . saw Isaac caressing Rebekah: The word for “caressing” (Hebrew metsakheq) is the same as the word used for Ishmael’s “making fun of” Isaac (Genesis 21:9); the word is related to the name “Isaac” (Hebrew yitskhaq). It is as though Isaac’s lapse of faith made fun of Abimelech and made a mockery of Rebekah and the great promise embodied in Isaac’s name.

Isaac, like his father, was rebuked by Abimelech (see study note on 20:1-18). This legal wording would remind Israel of how important it was to preserve marital purity. Abimelech recognized the danger to his own people. Though his decree preserved his own society, it was also a word from God that preserved the sanctity of Isaac’s and Israel’s marriages. If Isaac’s marriage had ended here, there would have been no Israelite society.
Isaac lived in the land as a temporary settler, enjoying abundant prosperity because of God’s blessing; his crops flourished and he became very rich.
The Philistines envied Isaac’s prosperity and filled his wells with dirt. The king then ordered Isaac to leave that region because he was too powerful for them (cp. Genesis 21:22-23).

Isaac moved . . . to the Gerar Valley (away from the city of Gerar itself, Genesis 26:6, but probably still within ten miles) and reopened his father’s wells. Isaac was also opposed there, but chose not to fight back; he relinquished one well after another until God’s blessing outdid the opposition. Whenever Isaac reopened a well, and regardless of how often enemies caused them to cave in, he found water. God was blessing Isaac and that blessing could not be hindered. Finally, the Philistines left Isaac alone.

At Beersheba, . . . the Lord appeared to Isaac to confirm his covenant (cp. Genesis 21:31-33). Isaac responded in faith as his father had done by building an altar to the Lord and proclaiming the Lord’s identity and nature (see study note on 12:8; Genesis 21:33).

This treaty is similar to the one an earlier king had made with Abraham (cp. Genesis 21:22-31). This king acknowledged that God was blessing Isaac and realized that a treaty with Isaac would benefit him. No opposition can hinder God’s blessing—it will flourish, and other nations will see it and seek peace with God’s people to share in the blessing.
Since the earlier treaty was renewed with Isaac, the name of the well was also renewed by the oath.

Esau’s marriages illustrate how unfit he was to lead the covenant people into God’s blessings, and how foolish was Isaac’s later attempt to bless Esau (Genesis 27:1-40). Esau later married a third wife in a vain attempt to do the right thing (Genesis 28:6-9).

The first scene sets up the chapter’s crisis. Isaac knew of God’s oracle (Genesis 25:22-23), yet he thwarted or ignored it by trying to bless Esau. • Isaac was old and turning blind: He was losing his senses, both physically and spiritually.

Jacob got his father Isaac’s blessing through deception. In this story, an entire family tries to carry out their responsibilities by physical means rather than by faith. Faith would have provided Rebekah and Jacob a more honorable solution to the crisis.
Like Esau, Isaac allowed his palate to govern his heart (cp. Genesis 25:28-34).
Esau agreed to Isaac’s plan, thus breaking the oath he had sworn to Jacob (Genesis 25:33).

The blessing seemed to be in jeopardy. In scene two, Rebekah and Jacob sought to achieve God’s blessing by deception, without faith or love. Rebekah planned to deceive the old man into thinking that he was blessing Esau when he was actually blessing Jacob.
Jacob had no qualms about this deception; he only feared that it might not work and that he would be cursed for trying.
Jacob lied about his identity, and then came close to blasphemy by lying about God.
In scene three, Jacob deceives his father and receives the blessing.
Isaac voiced his suspicion three times but was finally deceived by his senses, which were not functioning well (see study note on 27:1-4).
In scene four, everything is discovered, and the family becomes even more divided.
When he realized what had happened, Isaac began to tremble uncontrollably; he had been tampering with God’s plan, and God had overruled him.
Esau was very bitter, and angry enough to kill (Genesis 27:41).

Esau began to realize Jacob’s true nature, saying he has cheated me (or tripped me up, or deceived me) twice, by taking the birthright (the right of inheritance, Hebrew bekorah; Genesis 25:27-34) and by deceiving their father to receive the blessing (the spoken pronouncement of the inheritance, Hebrew berakah). • Esau’s assessment of Jacob was correct, but he failed to see his own ungodliness in these transactions (see study note on 27:5; Hebrews 12:16).
There was no going back. Isaac had declared an oracle from God, who had made Jacob to be Esau’s master (see Romans 9:11-13).
All that remained for Esau was a promise of hardship and struggle (cp. Genesis 3:17-19; Genesis 16:11-12).

Rebekah and Jacob got the blessing but reaped hatred from Esau and separation from one another; there is no indication that Rebekah and Jacob ever saw each other again. They gained nothing that God was not already going to give them, and their methods were costly. Jacob fled from home to escape Esau’s vengeance.

Jacob met the Lord on a route that Abraham had taken 125 years earlier. The story recounted in Genesis 27:42–33:17 follows a chiastic structure that centers on Jacob’s exile: A: Jacob flees Esau (Genesis 27:42–28:9) B: Angels of God meet Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:10-22) C: Jacob is exiled in Paddan-aram (Genesis 29:1–31:55) B’: Angels of God meet Jacob at Mahanaim (Genesis 32:1-2) A’: Jacob is reconciled to Esau (Genesis 32:3–33:17).
Rebekah manipulated Isaac into sending Jacob away. Like Isaac, Jacob took a wife from among his relatives in the east.

Isaac remained in the land, but Jacob had to leave it. God would deal with Jacob under the hand of Laban, his uncle (see study note on 29:1–31:55). • Believers in any age must remain spiritually pure by marrying other believers (2 Cor 6:14-18). The Canaanite people incorporated dozens of groups and clans into their society and religion by wars, treaties, and marriages (see Genesis 34:20-23). Abraham’s family was to resist such mixing (cp. Genesis 24:3; ch Genesis 34:1-31); they were to marry within their clan to maintain the purity of the line and of the faith that identified them as the chosen seed. The surest way to lose their distinctiveness was to intermarry with people of other tribal backgrounds and beliefs (see Ezra 9:1–10:44; Nehemiah 13:23-29).

Before Jacob departed, Isaac gave him a pure, legitimate blessing. He did not hold back, because he now knew what God wanted him to do. Isaac clearly passed on the blessing God Almighty (Hebrew El-Shaddai; see Genesis 17:1) had given to Abraham and to him regarding prosperity and the land (cp. Genesis 15:5, Genesis 15:18-20).

Esau, the unchosen son still trying to please his father, married a woman from the unchosen line of Ishmael, which he thought would be more acceptable. He did not understand the uniqueness of the covenant family.

Despite Jacob’s previous means of securing the blessing, God assured him of protection and provision. The God of Abraham and Isaac was also the God of Jacob. The revelation dramatically changed Jacob’s outlook and brought faith into clearer focus.
The good place where Jacob set up camp was apparently a protected area at the foot of a hill. The stone to rest his head against was probably large, more for protection than for a pillow.

stairway (traditionally ladder): This word occurs nowhere else in Scripture. The imagery probably reminded readers of a staircase or ramp up the front of a ziggurat that signified communication between heaven and earth (see study note on 11:4). God initiated a divine communication between heaven and earth to guide and protect Jacob, the steward of his covenant (Genesis 28:13-15; see Psalm 91:11-15). • Jesus said that he himself is the stairway between heaven and earth (John 1:51).

The point of the vision was that God and his angels were with Jacob on his journey. God reiterated to Jacob the covenant promises made to Abraham and Isaac, promising him land, descendants numerous as the dust (cp. Genesis 13:16; Genesis 22:17), and universal blessing through him (cp. Genesis 12:2-3; Genesis 15:5, Genesis 15:18; Genesis 17:3-8; Genesis 22:15-18; Genesis 35:11-12). God also promised to be with Jacob and watch over him until he returned.
Jacob inherited Abraham’s entire covenant (see Genesis 22:17), which confirmed Isaac’s blessing (Genesis 28:3-4) and stipulated a temporary exile (Genesis 28:15; see Genesis 15:12-16).

I am with you: The promise of God’s presence meant that God would protect and provide for Jacob in a special way. God’s promise to be with his people is repeated throughout Scripture (see also Genesis 26:24), prompting a response of worship and confidence in those who have faith (Genesis 28:16-22).

The second half of the passage gives Jacob’s response to the revelation. He felt reverential fear and awe in the Lord’s presence, and his acts of devotion became archetypes of Israel’s worship. When God graciously visits his people and promises to be with them and make them a blessing to the world, his people respond in faith with reverential fear, worship, offerings, and vows. They preserve their faith in memory for future worshipers.
Anointing with oil became a way of setting something apart for divine use in Israel’s worship (Exodus 29:1-7; Exodus 40:9; Leviticus 2:1; 1 Sam 10:1).
Bethel later became a holy site for Israel (see Judges 20:18-27; 1 Sam 7:16; 10:3; 1 Kgs 12:26–13:10; 2 Kgs 2:2-3).

In view of what God would do for him, Jacob vowed to do certain things for God. He believed the Lord’s words and responded in gratitude. Jacob’s vow influenced Israel’s way of making commitments to God in worship.

I will present to God a tenth: By paying a tithe (a tenth) as an act of worship, a person acknowledges that everything is a gift from God and belongs to God (see Genesis 14:19-20; Numbers 18:21-32; Deuteronomy 14:22-29; 2 Chr 31:5-6; Malachi 3:7-12; Matthew 23:23).

Jacob hurried on: The Hebrew text says that he “picked up his feet” as if he felt the wind at his back; he continued his journey with fresh enthusiasm. His changed outlook was the direct result of the vision he received at Bethel, a marvelous revelation that God was going to protect and bless him. He now sought the fulfillment of God’s promises to him, not just an escape from Esau. Jacob’s attitude had become positive and magnanimous to the point of being naive and vulnerable.

These chapters tell how God kept his promise by abundantly blessing Jacob with family and possessions. God also disciplined Jacob, leaving him to struggle with Laban for many years. Laban was Jacob’s match in deception, and thus a means of correction. • The story of Jacob and Laban parallels Israel’s later sojourn in Egypt. Jacob struggled while serving his uncle but finally emerged with a large family (the founders of the twelve tribes) and great wealth. In Egypt, the Israelites suffered under their oppressors, but they also flourished, becoming a great nation of twelve large tribes and escaping with great riches.

Jacob’s meeting Rachel at the well was providentially timed by the sovereign God who was leading Jacob to fulfillment of the promises (cp. Genesis 24:12-20). The well was a reminder of God’s blessing (cp. Genesis 16:13-14; Genesis 21:19; Genesis 26:19-25, Genesis 26:33).

In contrast to the lazy, unhelpful shepherds (Genesis 29:7-8), Jacob is portrayed as generous, industrious, and energetic. • Jacob . . . watered his uncle’s flock: Laban’s flocks would flourish under Jacob’s care.
Jacob kissed Rachel: Kissing relatives was a proper greeting (Genesis 29:13; cp. Song of Solomon 8:1).
You really are my own flesh and blood! Laban welcomed Jacob into his house and treated him much like a son.

Jacob’s joyful prospect of marriage to the lovely Rachel became an occasion for Laban’s shrewdness and Jacob’s discipline. Jacob and his mother had deceived his father and brother to gain the blessing; now his mother’s brother deceived him. Jacob received a dose of his own duplicity through twenty years of labor, affliction, and deception in Laban’s service (Genesis 31:38). In God’s justice, people harvest what they plant (Galatians 6:7). Laban’s deception was perfectly designed to make Jacob aware of his own craftiness. God often brings people into the lives of believers to discipline them. But Jacob was tenacious, and God blessed him abundantly with a large family and many possessions (Genesis 30:25-43) during this time of service.
Seven years of service was a high bride-price in the ancient world, but Rachel was beautiful (like Sarah and Rebekah), and Jacob was in love with her.

Like Isaac, Jacob was plied with food and wine (cp. Genesis 27:25), deprived of sight in the darkness (cp. Genesis 27:1), baffled by clothing (cp. Genesis 27:15), and misled by touch (cp. Genesis 27:23). The marriage had been consummated (Genesis 29:23; see Genesis 2:24), so Jacob was bound to Leah. • It’s not our custom here to marry off a younger daughter ahead of the firstborn: Laban’s words are a reminder of what Jacob did when he, the younger son, pretended to be his older brother to gain the blessing (ch Genesis 27:1-46). Now Leah, the older sister, pretended to be the younger sister to get a husband. God gave the deceiver a dose of his own deception as a discipline in his life.

After the bridal week ended (Genesis 29:27), Jacob also received Rachel as his wife, though he then would have to work an additional seven years (cp. Genesis 31:41). Laban seemed to have gained the upper hand.

Jacob loved Rachel much more than Leah: Favoritism was an ongoing cause of dysfunction in Jacob’s family (cp. Genesis 25:28; Genesis 37:3). Jacob’s favoritism had lasting effects: his family was never together, and their descendants, the tribes of Israel, were rarely unified.

Leah’s first four sons were born in rapid succession, but Rachel could not conceive. She was barren, like Sarah and Rebekah (cp. Genesis 16:1; Genesis 25:21; see also 1 Sam 1:1-28; Luke 1:5-25). • Each name is a memorable wordplay on Leah’s experience and hopes.

The rivalry between these sisters explains much of the later rivalry among their sons, and then among the tribes, just as the rivalry between Jacob and Laban foreshadowed conflict between Israel and the Arameans of Damascus (2 Sam 8:5-6; 10:8-19; 1 Kgs 20:1-34; 2 Kgs 5:1–8:29; 13:1-25; Isaiah 7:1-9). • God champions the cause of the poor and oppressed; he exalted Leah, the despised first wife, as the first to become a mother. Judah’s kingly tribe and Levi’s priestly line came through her despite Jacob’s favoritism for Rachel and her children. Despite the tension and jealousy resulting from Laban’s treachery and Jacob’s favoritism, God still built Jacob’s family and brought about the births of the tribal ancestors.

Reuben (Hebrew re’uben) sounds like the Hebrew for “He has seen my misery” (ra‘ah be‘onyi). His birth gave Leah consolation from God and hope for Jacob’s love. Jacob seems not to have seen her misery, but God did (cp. Genesis 16:14; Genesis 24:62; Genesis 25:11). The name was a reminder of God’s intervention.
Leah named her second son Simeon. The name suggests that she had cried out to the Lord and was heard (cp. Genesis 16:11).
Leah named her third son Levi, hoping that her husband would become “attached” to her since she had given him three sons. This hope was not fulfilled.

Leah reconciled herself to the reality that nothing would turn Jacob’s affections toward her. She named her fourth son Judah with the sentiment, “I will praise the Lord.” She seems to have given up on Jacob, taking her consolation from the Lord.
In that culture, it was like death for a woman not to have children (cp. 1 Sam 1); only God could open Rachel’s womb.

Rachel’s naming of sons through Bilhah does not reflect faith as Leah’s namings had. Rachel felt wronged over the marriage and her barrenness. The names of Bilhah’s sons reflect Rachel’s bitter struggle with her sister and her feeling of some victory.
Rachel’s decision to have children through her servant, and Jacob’s compliance, recall Sarai’s use of Hagar (Genesis 16:1-4).
Dan means “he judged” or “he vindicated.” Rachel felt vindicated (Hebrew dananni) by Dan’s birth.
The name Naphtali is related to the clause I have struggled hard (Hebrew naptule ’elohim niptalti, “I have struggled the struggles of God”).
When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, she countered Rachel’s effort by giving her servant . . . to Jacob as a wife even though she already had four sons.
Gad was the name of a god of fortune. Asher was the name of a god of luck. These names reflect Leah’s pagan background, but there is no indication that she believed in these gods.

Mandrakes were considered an aphrodisiac and aid to procreation (see Song of Solomon 7:13). Rachel thought they would help her get pregnant, so she traded Jacob for a night to get them. In the process, Leah got pregnant, not Rachel.
The name Issachar captures the sense of Jacob’s being hired (Genesis 30:16) and of the Lord’s rewarding Leah (Hebrew sekari, “my hire”).
Zebulun means “honor” or “gift,” as in a dowry or tribute. Leah thought that God gave her Zebulun so that her husband would honor her. This hope never fully left her.
Dinah was Jacob’s only daughter. See ch Genesis 34:1-31.

Rachel finally gave birth to her own son, Joseph. His birth was brought about by God’s intervention, not by superstitious practices (Genesis 30:14-16) or the social custom of giving servants as wives. • Removed (Hebrew ’asap, “take away”) sounds similar to Joseph (Hebrew yosep, “may he add”). Rachel rejoiced over Joseph’s birth, yet she prayed that the Lord would add yet another son to her family.

After his fourteen years of service, Jacob asked Laban for permission to go home. The two bedouin leaders negotiated politely but remained cautiously on guard. Laban wanted to get more out of Jacob. Jacob wanted to gain his wages by selective breeding.

I have become wealthy: God had prospered Laban through Jacob’s presence (see Genesis 22:18). Laban may have looked for omens, or simply have perceived what was happening. Since dark-colored sheep (Genesis 30:32) were rare, a large number of them was considered an omen of God’s blessing.

Jacob agreed that God had blessed Laban through him, so he made a plan to gain something for himself. He proposed for his wages the rare black and multicolored goats and the speckled and spotted sheep that were born.

As Abraham had done with Lot (Genesis 13:9), Jacob gave Laban what he valued most. White sheep were more common and more valuable than dark or multicolored sheep; as a man of faith, Jacob was willing to take the rejects (cp. 1 Cor 1:26).

Laban verbally agreed with Jacob’s plan, but he tried to prevent Jacob from accruing wealth by removing animals from the flock that would fulfill the agreement. • Laban’s deception with his goats reminds us of Jacob’s deception of Esau (cp. Genesis 27:9; see study note on 29:14-30).

making white streaks: A clever wordplay captures the meaning of this whole section. When Jacob exposed the white (Hebrew laban) streaks of wood underneath, he played the “white” game (the Laban game) and won. As he outwitted Laban (“Whitey”), Jacob’s flocks flourished and Jacob prospered.

God blessed Jacob despite Laban’s duplicity. Not to be outwitted, Jacob used selective breeding to acquire a flock, following the traditional belief that peeled sticks influenced the kind of animal that would be born. The peeled branches seemingly made his animals produce streaked and spotted young; Jacob later acknowledged that God had prospered him (Genesis 31:7-12). Jacob gained stronger animals for himself and weaker ones for Laban (Genesis 30:41-42).
Laban now received due recompense for his treatment of Jacob. Laban’s attempt to defraud Jacob resulted in Jacob’s coming out ahead, because God was at work in his life.
Jacob became very wealthy, in fulfillment of God’s promises to him (Genesis 27:28; Genesis 28:13-15).

The animosity of Laban’s sons against Jacob grew because his flocks were multiplying faster than Laban’s. They were jealous of God’s blessing on Jacob and afraid that he would completely overrun them.

Jacob’s return journey precipitated a confrontation with Laban that set a permanent boundary between Israel (Jacob) and Aram (Laban). God kept his word to Jacob by prospering him in Paddan-aram and protecting him on his journey home.

The land of your father and grandfather was the land of Canaan, to which Abraham had previously been called (Genesis 12:1-7; Genesis 17:8). • Return . . . I will be with you: See study notes on 26:2-5; 28:12-15. God protected Jacob (“Israel,” Genesis 32:28) as he brought his family back to the land that was promised to them. God later brought Israel back to Canaan after long years of service in Egypt. That great return had many elements similar to this passage: God defeated foreign gods and beliefs, used dreams for rescue and protection, gave victory over those who threatened them, and established boundaries between nations and tribes (see Deuteronomy 32:8).

Jacob explained to his wives how God had blessed him despite Laban’s opposition. He was not sure they would want to leave Laban and go to Canaan. He wanted to take a willing family, so he had to make an effective appeal.
